questions.question: In 1935 Erwin Schrödinger published a thought experiment in *Naturwissenschaften*. A cat in a sealed box is linked to a radioactive atom through a vial of poison — if the atom decays, the vial breaks. According to a literal reading of quantum mechanics, before you open the box, what state is the cat in? Schrödinger was making a point, not a prediction.
questions.answer: A superposition of alive and dead — which Schrödinger thought was absurd, showing the theory was incomplete in some way
choices: A superposition of alive and dead — which Schrödinger thought was absurd, showing the theory was incomplete in some way
Definitely dead — radioactive decay always happens within minutes of the atom being placed in the box arrangement
Definitely alive — quantum effects vanish for any object larger than a single atom, by an unknown size threshold
In a known classical state — the box itself measures the atom and collapses any superposition before opening
questions.context: Schrödinger devised the cat to mock the Copenhagen interpretation of his Vienna colleagues, who held that quantum systems exist in superposition until measured. He thought it absurd to apply that to a cat. Decades later, the question of where the quantum-to-classical boundary lives remains unresolved — interpretations include Copenhagen, Many-Worlds (Everett 1957), decoherence, and others. No experiment has yet decisively chosen between them.

questions.question: In May 1935 Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen published a paper in *Physical Review* arguing that quantum mechanics could not be a complete description of reality. Their argument used pairs of particles whose properties were correlated. What did EPR conclude was wrong with quantum mechanics?
questions.answer: Either it was incomplete — missing 'hidden variables' that determine outcomes — or it required 'spooky action at a distance,' which they considered absurd
choices: Either it was incomplete — missing 'hidden variables' that determine outcomes — or it required 'spooky action at a distance,' which they considered absurd
It was mathematically inconsistent — different calculations of the same observable would yield different predicted results in every experimental setup
It violated energy conservation — measurements would create or destroy energy in ways that ordinary mechanics could never reproduce
It applied only to single particles — multi-particle systems could not be described by quantum mechanics at all even in principle
questions.context: Einstein's phrase 'spukhafte Fernwirkung' ('spooky action at a distance') captured his discomfort. He preferred local hidden variables: each particle carries its own pre-determined answer, and measurement just reveals it. Niels Bohr replied within months, defending the Copenhagen view. The debate could not be settled by argument — but in 1964 John Bell showed it could be settled by experiment.

questions.question: In 1964 Northern Irish physicist John Bell, working at CERN, published a short paper showing that any theory with local hidden variables had to obey a specific mathematical inequality. Quantum mechanics predicts that inequality is violated. What did Bell's theorem turn the Einstein–Bohr debate into?
questions.answer: An experimentally testable question — measurements could now distinguish between local hidden variables and quantum mechanics in a laboratory setting
choices: An experimentally testable question — measurements could now distinguish between local hidden variables and quantum mechanics in a laboratory setting
A purely mathematical exercise — no real-world experiment could ever bear on the question one way or the other
A settled question — Bell had proven Einstein was right that hidden variables exist beneath the quantum surface
A settled question — Bell had proven Bohr was right by deriving Copenhagen from completely independent first principles
questions.context: Bell's paper, 'On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen Paradox,' appeared in the short-lived journal *Physics Physique Fizika* because he wanted no page charges. The 'Bell inequality' is a constraint that any local-hidden-variable theory must satisfy. Quantum mechanics predicts entangled particles violate it. For nearly two decades after 1964, the experiment was technically out of reach.

questions.question: Between 1980 and 1982 French physicist Alain Aspect, at the Institut d'Optique near Paris, ran the first conclusive tests of Bell's inequality using pairs of entangled photons. By his third experiment he switched polarizer orientations while photons were already in flight, closing the 'locality loophole.' What did his measurements show?
questions.answer: The inequality was violated by the amount quantum mechanics predicted — ruling out the kind of local hidden variables Einstein had hoped existed beneath the quantum picture
choices: The inequality was violated by the amount quantum mechanics predicted — ruling out the kind of local hidden variables Einstein had hoped existed beneath the quantum picture
The inequality held exactly — confirming Einstein's local hidden variables and refuting quantum mechanics in its standard form altogether
The inequality could not be tested — entangled photon pairs cannot be reliably produced in any laboratory setting using current optical equipment
The inequality was violated by an amount no theory predicted — leaving the question entirely open even as recently as the early 2020s
questions.context: Aspect's 1982 paper in *Physical Review Letters* was a landmark. Local hidden variables — Einstein's preferred escape — were experimentally ruled out for the kind of correlations entangled particles show. Aspect shared the 2022 Nobel in Physics with John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger 'for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities, and pioneering quantum information science.'

questions.question: The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Alain Aspect, John Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger. Their experiments confirmed something Einstein had hoped was not true and laid the foundation for a new technological field. What field?
questions.answer: Quantum information science — including quantum cryptography, quantum teleportation of states between particles, and the early steps toward quantum computing
choices: Quantum information science — including quantum cryptography, quantum teleportation of states between particles, and the early steps toward quantum computing
Cold-fusion research — including the tabletop reactor designs piloted in the 1990s and revived periodically through the 2000s with controversial results
String theory — including the prediction of supersymmetric partner particles for every known elementary particle and their direct detection at the LHC
Stellar nucleosynthesis — including the formation of elements heavier than iron inside supernovae and the production of gold during neutron-star mergers
questions.context: Quantum teleportation transmits the state of one particle to another without moving the particle itself. Quantum key distribution (BB84, Bennett and Brassard 1984) uses the no-cloning property of quantum states to make eavesdropping detectable. Zeilinger's group demonstrated quantum teleportation in 1997. The Nobel committee specifically honored the path from foundational paradox to working technology.

questions.question: The Standard Model of particle physics, largely completed by the mid-1970s, classifies the known elementary particles into three groups: matter particles (quarks and leptons), force-carrier particles (photon, gluon, W and Z bosons), and the Higgs boson. What's the most famous thing the Standard Model does NOT explain?
questions.answer: Gravity — there is no Standard Model description, and its quantum theory has resisted formulation for over half a century of sustained effort
choices: Gravity — there is no Standard Model description, and its quantum theory has resisted formulation for over half a century of sustained effort
Electromagnetism — the model treats it only as a classical field with no quantum description and no carrier particle of any kind
Radioactive decay — the model has no place for the weak nuclear force, beta decay, or any of the related transformations of matter
Color charge — the model includes no theory of how quarks bind into protons and neutrons, leaving that mechanism completely unexplained
questions.context: The Standard Model is one of the most precise theories in physics: its predictions for the electron's magnetic moment match measurements to about one part in a trillion. But it does not include gravity, does not explain dark matter or dark energy, and does not explain why there is more matter than antimatter. These are the headline open problems modern physicists work on.

questions.question: On July 4, 2012, two independent detector teams at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, ATLAS and CMS, announced their discovery at a press conference in Geneva. A British theoretical physicist watched the announcement and wept. What had they found, and who was the man?
questions.answer: The Higgs boson — and Peter Higgs, who had proposed its existence in 1964 and waited 48 years for experimental confirmation of his prediction
choices: The Higgs boson — and Peter Higgs, who had proposed its existence in 1964 and waited 48 years for experimental confirmation of his prediction
A magnetic monopole — and Paul Dirac, who had proposed their existence in 1931 and watched the field debate them for over four decades
The graviton — and Bryce DeWitt, who had quantized gravity in his 1967 paper and pursued a quantum theory of gravity for many years
A magnetic monopole partner — and Pierre Ramond, who had proposed such particles in 1971 as part of an early extension of the Standard Model framework
questions.context: The Higgs field gives elementary particles their mass through interactions with the field; particles that interact strongly with it (like top quarks) are heavy, particles that don't (like photons) are massless. Peter Higgs, François Englert, and Robert Brout had proposed the mechanism in 1964 (Brout died in 2011, before the discovery). Higgs and Englert shared the 2013 Nobel in Physics.

questions.question: Murray Gell-Mann at Caltech and George Zweig at CERN independently proposed in 1964 that protons and neutrons were not elementary, but built from three smaller particles each. Gell-Mann named them after a nonsense word from James Joyce's *Finnegans Wake*: 'Three quarks for Muster Mark!' What's the recognition skill here?
questions.answer: What looks elementary in one generation of physics is often shown to be composite in the next — proton-as-elementary-particle gave way to proton-as-three-quarks within a single century
choices: What looks elementary in one generation of physics is often shown to be composite in the next — proton-as-elementary-particle gave way to proton-as-three-quarks within a single century
Particle physics names always come from medieval Latin manuscripts — they have no twentieth-century or modern literary origins of any kind, despite occasional rumors otherwise
Gell-Mann was wrong about quarks — his 1964 proposal was formally retracted by him personally in 1969 and replaced with an alternative substructure theory
Quarks are purely mathematical objects — they have no detectable physical effects on any experiment and remain undetected even by the most sensitive modern instruments
questions.context: Direct evidence for quarks came from deep-inelastic-scattering experiments at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC) in 1968-1969, which showed protons had a hard sub-structure (Friedman, Kendall, Taylor, Nobel 1990). Six quark flavors exist (up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom). They are bound by the strong force, carried by gluons. They have never been observed in isolation — confinement holds them together.

questions.question: The electron is the most familiar lepton. The Standard Model includes six leptons in three 'generations' — electron, muon, tau, and their three matching neutrinos. The muon was discovered in 1936 in cosmic rays and at first mistaken for the predicted Yukawa pion. What did Nobel laureate I.I. Rabi famously ask when the muon was identified as a separate particle?
questions.answer: 'Who ordered that?' — capturing the puzzle that nature contains heavy copies of the electron with no obvious purpose or place in the picture
choices: 'Who ordered that?' — capturing the puzzle that nature contains heavy copies of the electron with no obvious purpose or place in the picture
'It cannot be real' — capturing his initial belief that the discovery had to be an experimental error in detection, calibration, or analysis
'Where is the proton?' — capturing his concern that no positively charged counterpart particle had been observed alongside the new neutral lepton
'How fast does it spin?' — capturing his interest in the new particle's angular momentum properties and the question of its statistics
questions.context: Why nature has three generations of matter, all with the same charges but different masses, is one of the Standard Model's open puzzles. The top quark, the heaviest known elementary particle, weighs as much as a tungsten atom. Why? No one knows. The mass hierarchy is taken as given.

questions.question: The Standard Model describes four forces but covers only three. Each described force is carried by a specific kind of particle, exchanged between matter particles. Photons carry electromagnetism. What carries the strong force that binds quarks into protons, and the weak force responsible for some radioactive decay?
questions.answer: Gluons carry the strong force — and W and Z bosons carry the weak force, all confirmed by experiments at CERN and elsewhere through the 1970s and 1980s
choices: Gluons carry the strong force — and W and Z bosons carry the weak force, all confirmed by experiments at CERN and elsewhere through the 1970s and 1980s
Gravitons carry the strong force — and neutrinos carry the weak force, both detected at the LEP collider at CERN during 1989 calibration runs
Higgs bosons carry the strong force — and muons carry the weak force, both confirmed independently at the LHC during the 2012 discovery announcements
The strong and weak forces have no carrier particles — they act directly between matter particles without any exchange particle mediating between them
questions.context: Gluons (Brodsky, Schwitters et al. confirmation at PETRA 1979) come in eight 'color' types and bind quarks. W and Z bosons (Rubbia and van der Meer at CERN, 1983 — Nobel 1984) mediate the weak force, with the W carrying electric charge and the Z neutral. The fourth force, gravity, has no confirmed Standard Model carrier; the predicted 'graviton' remains hypothetical.

questions.question: Two independent teams — the Supernova Cosmology Project led by Saul Perlmutter at Berkeley and the High-Z Supernova Search led by Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess — published results in 1998 and 1999 that overturned the previous expectation. What had cosmologists expected, and what did the measurements show?
questions.answer: Expected the expansion to be slowing under gravity — but observed the expansion is accelerating, driven by some unknown component pushing the universe outward instead
choices: Expected the expansion to be slowing under gravity — but observed the expansion is accelerating, driven by some unknown component pushing the universe outward instead
Expected the universe to be static and unchanging — but observed the universe is expanding at the rate Hubble first measured back in his earliest 1929 paper
Expected the universe to be contracting toward a big crunch — but observed the universe is contracting much faster than any model since the 1970s had predicted
Expected the universe to be no older than four billion years — but observed the universe is at least one hundred billion years old based on supernova evidence
questions.context: Both teams used Type Ia supernovae as 'standard candles' — their intrinsic brightness can be calibrated, so apparent brightness gives distance. Distant supernovae appeared dimmer than a decelerating universe would have produced. Perlmutter, Schmidt, and Riess shared the 2011 Nobel in Physics. The unknown driver was named 'dark energy' and makes up about 68% of the universe's energy content. We don't know what it is.

questions.question: Quantum field theory predicts that empty space should contain vacuum energy. The simplest prediction overestimates the actual cosmological-constant value by about 10^120 — that is, 1 followed by 120 zeros. Physicists call it 'the worst theoretical prediction in the history of physics.' What does this catastrophic mismatch tell us?
questions.answer: Something fundamental about how vacuum energy and gravity combine — the gap is too large to dismiss as ordinary error and points to missing physics in our current theories
choices: Something fundamental about how vacuum energy and gravity combine — the gap is too large to dismiss as ordinary error and points to missing physics in our current theories
Quantum field theory has been entirely refuted — no modern physicist uses it after the 1998 discovery, and it was replaced by alternative non-quantum frameworks
The discrepancy disappears entirely — when you use units other than those Planck originally chose, the predicted and observed values agree to four significant digits
The vacuum energy was directly measured — a 2014 detection matched quantum-field-theory predictions exactly and showed no remaining discrepancy in modern physics
questions.context: The cosmological constant problem is one of the deepest open puzzles in physics. Some physicists suspect a cancellation between positive and negative contributions to vacuum energy; others suspect the anthropic principle (we live in a universe with a small constant because larger constants would prevent galaxies from forming). Neither has decisive support. The honest answer is: we don't know why the constant is so small.

questions.question: The cosmic microwave background, predicted by Gamow's team in the 1940s and discovered accidentally by Penzias and Wilson at Bell Labs in 1965, is the afterglow of the early universe. Three space missions — COBE (1989), WMAP (2001), and Planck (2009) — have measured its temperature variations with steadily increasing precision. What did the measurements confirm?
questions.answer: The Big Bang model — the universe was once hot and dense, cooled as it expanded, and is now about 13.8 billion years old as best as the precision data can determine
choices: The Big Bang model — the universe was once hot and dense, cooled as it expanded, and is now about 13.8 billion years old as best as the precision data can determine
The Steady State model — the universe has always existed in roughly its current form, with continuous creation of matter to maintain density as space expands
Galaxy-rotation models — the visible mass alone is enough to hold galaxies together, requiring no dark matter or modified gravity in their underlying theory
Cyclic universe models — the universe has been through dozens of bounces with alternating hot and cool phases that observers can trace back through CMB data
questions.context: The CMB has a temperature of about 2.7 kelvin and the spectrum of a near-perfect black body. Tiny temperature variations (one part in 100,000) seeded the formation of galaxies. The pattern of these variations matches the Big Bang model with cold dark matter and dark energy to extraordinary precision. COBE leaders John Mather and George Smoot shared the 2006 Nobel in Physics.

questions.question: On September 14, 2015, the twin Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) detectors at Hanford, Washington and Livingston, Louisiana picked up a signal lasting about a fifth of a second. The announcement came in February 2016. What had they detected?
questions.answer: Gravitational waves from two black holes — they had spiraled into each other about 1.3 billion light-years away, in the first direct detection of such waves in history
choices: Gravitational waves from two black holes — they had spiraled into each other about 1.3 billion light-years away, in the first direct detection of such waves in history
Neutrinos from the Sun's core — marking the first direct detection of solar neutrinos at LIGO sites since the Davis underground experiment back in 1968
Radio pulses from an unknown pulsar — the first pulsar observation to be conclusively recorded simultaneously by both northern and southern hemisphere instruments
Cosmic rays from an unknown source — the first detection of ultra-high-energy events ever recorded by both terrestrial detectors at the same instant
questions.context: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein in 1916. LIGO's detectors are L-shaped interferometers with arms 4 kilometers long. Their detection required measuring length changes thousands of times smaller than the diameter of a proton. The September 2015 signal matched general relativity's prediction for a merger of black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses. Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, and Barry Barish shared the 2017 Nobel in Physics.

questions.question: On August 17, 2017, LIGO and Virgo detected gravitational waves from a different kind of event — and about two seconds later, NASA's Fermi space telescope picked up a gamma-ray burst from the same patch of sky. Optical telescopes pinpointed the source within hours. What had collided, and why was the multi-messenger detection important?
questions.answer: Two neutron stars merged in galaxy NGC 4993 — and the simultaneous gravitational, gamma, optical and infrared signals confirmed neutron-star mergers produce heavy elements like gold and platinum
choices: Two neutron stars merged in galaxy NGC 4993 — and the simultaneous gravitational, gamma, optical and infrared signals confirmed neutron-star mergers produce heavy elements like gold and platinum
Two galaxies collided in the Andromeda cluster — and the simultaneous detection was the first time astronomers had observed gravitational waves on a truly galactic scale
A black hole swallowed a planet in our own Milky Way — and the simultaneous detection was the first time such an event had been observed inside our home galaxy directly
A pulsar collided with a magnetar near Centaurus A — and the joint gamma-and-radio observation was the first to combine multiple detection types for a single localized event
questions.context: GW170817 was a landmark for 'multi-messenger astronomy' — combining gravitational waves with electromagnetic signals. The kilonova afterglow let astronomers measure heavy-element production directly. About 16,000 Earth masses of strontium and several Earth masses of gold and platinum were produced in the seconds-to-days following the merger.

questions.question: The Hubble constant H0 measures how fast the universe is expanding today. Two well-established methods give different answers: measurements from the cosmic microwave background suggest about 67-68 kilometers per second per megaparsec, while direct measurements from supernovae suggest about 73. The disagreement has grown more — not less — precise over time. What does this 'Hubble tension' suggest?
questions.answer: Either one method has an unrecognized systematic error — or our cosmological model is missing something, because the two measurements use different physics and the gap is now too large to dismiss
choices: Either one method has an unrecognized systematic error — or our cosmological model is missing something, because the two measurements use different physics and the gap is now too large to dismiss
Both methods are correct simultaneously — the Hubble constant is genuinely two different numbers at the same time, in different parts of the observable universe today
The CMB measurements have been retracted — only the supernova measurements are still considered valid by working cosmologists at major institutions since around 2020
The Hubble constant has been measured exactly — every cosmologist now agrees on a single value, and the apparent tension was an analysis error that has since been fully corrected
questions.context: The CMB measurement (Planck satellite, model-dependent) and the local distance ladder (Cepheids and supernovae, Adam Riess's SH0ES collaboration) have been refined for over a decade. JWST observations published since 2023 have so far supported the Cepheid-based measurements. Proposed solutions include new physics in the early universe (changed sound horizon), modified dark energy, or unrecognized systematic effects. Resolution is open.

questions.question: The James Webb Space Telescope launched in December 2021 and began returning data in 2022. Within months, observations showed galaxies appearing more massive and more mature than the standard cosmological model expected at very high redshift — that is, very early in cosmic history. What's the current state of the question?
questions.answer: The early-universe observations are real — but interpretations remain open, with proposals ranging from new physics to revised stellar-population models to better luminosity calibrations across the field
choices: The early-universe observations are real — but interpretations remain open, with proposals ranging from new physics to revised stellar-population models to better luminosity calibrations across the field
JWST has refuted the Big Bang model — most cosmologists now believe the universe has no beginning at all, and the framework of expanding-universe cosmology has been abandoned outright
JWST observations of early galaxies have all been shown to be artifacts — every paper claiming early galaxies was formally retracted by 2024 and the field has moved on entirely
JWST has confirmed the standard model perfectly — zero discrepancies of any kind have been reported across the full range of its observations from launch to the present day
questions.context: Headlines like 'JWST breaks cosmology' have been more dramatic than the underlying papers. Many early surprise findings have been moderated as analyses improved — but some tensions remain (high stellar masses at z>8, mature dust at z>10, possible 'little red dots'). The honest summary is that JWST is doing what new instruments often do: revealing that the standard model fits 99% but not 100%, and the 1% is interesting.

questions.question: In the 1970s American astronomer Vera Rubin, working with Kent Ford at the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism in Washington DC, measured the orbital speeds of stars in the outer regions of spiral galaxies. By Kepler's laws, stars far from the galactic center should orbit more slowly. What did Rubin find?
questions.answer: Outer stars orbit just as fast as inner stars — galaxies behave as if surrounded by halos of unseen mass that only gravity reveals, what we now call dark matter
choices: Outer stars orbit just as fast as inner stars — galaxies behave as if surrounded by halos of unseen mass that only gravity reveals, what we now call dark matter
Outer stars do not orbit at all — they drift freely through intergalactic space without being gravitationally bound to the home galaxy at all
Outer stars orbit exactly as Kepler predicted — confirming that the visible mass alone is enough to hold spiral galaxies together without any additional component
Outer stars cannot be reliably measured — spectroscopic techniques fail at large galactic radii, so their rotation rates remain unknown even today in the best surveys
questions.context: Rubin's measurements built on Fritz Zwicky's 1933 observation that the Coma cluster's galaxies were moving too fast to be bound by their visible mass. Rubin made the case unignorable. The Nobel committee did not award her a prize in her lifetime; she died in 2016. Dark matter has been inferred from many independent lines of evidence (galaxy clusters, CMB, gravitational lensing, structure formation) but has never been directly detected as a particle.

questions.question: Israeli physicist Mordehai Milgrom proposed in 1983 an alternative to dark matter called Modified Newtonian Dynamics, or MOND. Instead of adding unseen mass to galaxies, MOND modifies the law of gravity at very low accelerations. What's the current state of this debate?
questions.answer: MOND explains galaxy rotation curves with one parameter — but struggles with galaxy clusters and the CMB, so dark matter remains the consensus while the debate is not over
choices: MOND explains galaxy rotation curves with one parameter — but struggles with galaxy clusters and the CMB, so dark matter remains the consensus while the debate is not over
MOND has been definitively refuted — direct detection of dark-matter particles at the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment in 2018 closed the question to the satisfaction of every modified-gravity researcher
MOND has been confirmed and dark matter rejected — every major cosmologist has held this view since the Bullet Cluster, regardless of what some popular accounts state
MOND was retracted in 2002 by Milgrom himself — it is no longer considered a serious alternative by anyone working on galaxy dynamics or cluster astrophysics anywhere
questions.context: The Bullet Cluster (two colliding galaxy clusters where gravitational lensing seems to separate from visible gas) is widely cited as evidence for dark matter over MOND. But cluster simulations are not unambiguous, and recent variants like TeVeS (Bekenstein) and Verlinde's emergent gravity keep modified-gravity alive as a minority position. Honest reporting: the consensus favors dark matter, but the alternative has not been killed.

questions.question: In the first few minutes after the Big Bang, the universe was hot enough for nuclear fusion. The relative abundances of the lightest elements — hydrogen, helium, and trace lithium — that emerged from this period can be calculated. Observations of ancient stars and distant gas clouds match the prediction. What does this concordance support?
questions.answer: The Big Bang framework — observed abundances of primordial hydrogen, helium-4, deuterium, and helium-3 match the predicted ratios from nucleosynthesis in the first few minutes after the start
choices: The Big Bang framework — observed abundances of primordial hydrogen, helium-4, deuterium, and helium-3 match the predicted ratios from nucleosynthesis in the first few minutes after the start
The Steady State framework — observed abundances of all elements have been constant throughout cosmic time, with no nucleosynthesis-from-Big-Bang period detectable anywhere in the data
The MOND framework — observed abundances depend on modified gravity rather than on any primordial fusion period, and require no Big Bang nucleosynthesis at all to explain them
The Hoyle framework — observed elements were all produced in stars, none of them in the first few minutes of the universe, contrary to current modern Big Bang reasoning
questions.context: Primordial nucleosynthesis was worked out by George Gamow, Ralph Alpher, and Hans Bethe in the late 1940s — Gamow added Bethe to the author list for the 'alpha-beta-gamma' pun. Lithium-7 remains anomalous: predictions exceed observations by about a factor of three. This 'cosmological lithium problem' is unsolved but considered minor compared to dark matter or dark energy.

questions.question: In 1980 Alan Guth, then at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, proposed that the very early universe went through a brief period of exponential expansion — 'inflation' — lasting much less than a second. What problems was inflation designed to solve?
questions.answer: Why the CMB is uniform across regions — that should never have been in causal contact with each other, and why the geometry of space appears to be very nearly flat
choices: Why the CMB is uniform across regions — that should never have been in causal contact with each other, and why the geometry of space appears to be very nearly flat
Why galaxies rotate faster at their edges — than Kepler's laws would predict from their visible mass distribution, an unsolved problem since the time of Rubin
Why the cosmological constant is small but nonzero — rather than exactly zero as the simplest theoretical expectations from quantum field theory had originally suggested
Why dark matter and dark energy together add up to about 95% — of the total energy content of the universe today, dwarfing the visible matter we directly see
questions.context: Inflation has had remarkable success: it predicts the CMB power spectrum's main features (acoustic peaks, near-scale-invariance, near-flat geometry). But it remains unconfirmed at the particle-physics level — the 'inflaton' field has not been identified, and some physicists (Steinhardt, Ijjas, Loeb) argue inflation has become unfalsifiable due to its many model variants. The debate is active.

questions.question: In 1974 Stephen Hawking, then at Cambridge, published a paper arguing that black holes are not entirely black — they emit very faint thermal radiation due to quantum effects near the event horizon. Hawking himself called the result 'truly surprising.' What's the catch for an experimentalist hoping to detect this radiation?
questions.answer: Hawking radiation is too faint to detect from astrophysical black holes — for a solar-mass black hole the temperature is about a hundred-millionth of a kelvin, far below any conceivable instrument
choices: Hawking radiation is too faint to detect from astrophysical black holes — for a solar-mass black hole the temperature is about a hundred-millionth of a kelvin, far below any conceivable instrument
Hawking radiation has been routinely detected since the 1980s — using neutrino telescopes near major Cherenkov detectors at sites including IceCube and Super-Kamiokande over the years
Hawking radiation was formally retracted by Hawking himself in 1995 — it is no longer believed by any physicist working at the intersection of relativity and quantum theory today
Hawking radiation can only be detected from black holes more massive than the Milky Way's central black hole — making the prediction effectively untestable from Earth-based observatories
questions.context: Hawking's prediction depends on quantum field theory near a horizon, combining quantum mechanics and general relativity in a regime where each is well-tested separately. Laboratory analogs (Bose-Einstein condensates, optical fibers) have produced 'analog Hawking radiation' supporting the basic mechanism. Hawking never won a Nobel — the prize requires experimental confirmation, and his prediction has not been astronomically observed. The black-hole-information paradox his work raised remains unresolved.

questions.question: In 1867 James Clerk Maxwell described a thought-experiment 'demon' — a small intelligent being controlling a door between two gas chambers. By letting only fast molecules through one way and slow molecules the other, it could create a temperature difference from a uniform-temperature gas — seemingly violating the second law. What was the eventual resolution?
questions.answer: The demon must store information about each molecule — and erasing that information costs energy (Landauer 1961), so including the demon's records, total entropy still increases
choices: The demon must store information about each molecule — and erasing that information costs energy (Landauer 1961), so including the demon's records, total entropy still increases
The demon was shown to be physically possible by Maxwell — in his own 1879 paper, refuting the second law of thermodynamics permanently and changing the field forever
The demon was rejected as a logical contradiction — by Ludwig Boltzmann within months of the original proposal, and has not been considered a serious puzzle since then
The demon was confirmed in laboratory experiments at MIT in 2008 — and is now a working component of modern refrigerator designs across the consumer appliance industry
questions.context: Léo Szilárd's 1929 analysis introduced the link between information and thermodynamics. Rolf Landauer's 1961 principle — that erasing one bit of information requires at least kT·ln(2) of energy dissipated as heat — closed the puzzle. The episode is a key example of how a clever thought experiment can drive a century of progress in foundational physics.

questions.question: In 1824 French military engineer Sadi Carnot published *Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu*, the first systematic theory of heat engines. He showed that no engine operating between two temperatures can convert all the input heat into work — there's an absolute upper limit on efficiency. What did this result eventually become?
questions.answer: The second law of thermodynamics — the entropy of an isolated system never decreases, and the universe drifts irreversibly toward thermal equilibrium over very long time scales
choices: The second law of thermodynamics — the entropy of an isolated system never decreases, and the universe drifts irreversibly toward thermal equilibrium over very long time scales
The first law of thermodynamics — energy is neither created nor destroyed in any physical process, but only converted between different forms across the system as a whole
The zeroth law of thermodynamics — two systems in equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other, allowing temperature to be a well-defined and useful quantity
The third law of thermodynamics — the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is exactly zero, an unreachable limit that no laboratory cooling process can ever attain
questions.context: Carnot died of cholera in 1832 at age 36 — his single work was largely ignored until rediscovered by Émile Clapeyron in 1834 and developed by William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), Rudolf Clausius, and others into modern thermodynamics. Clausius coined the word 'entropy' in 1865. The second law's universality across systems from steam engines to galaxies remains one of physics's most striking results.

questions.question: Carnot's law applied to the universe as a whole gives a long-run prediction: if entropy is always increasing and energy spreads out, then the universe eventually reaches a state in which no further useful work can be extracted. This is often called the heat death. What does the dark-energy discovery of 1998 do to this scenario?
questions.answer: It strengthens it — with accelerating expansion, distant galaxies eventually leave each other's reachable horizons, and the long-run future looks colder, darker, and emptier than the simpler model had suggested
choices: It strengthens it — with accelerating expansion, distant galaxies eventually leave each other's reachable horizons, and the long-run future looks colder, darker, and emptier than the simpler model had suggested
It refutes it — with accelerating expansion, the universe will reach a high-energy hot equilibrium rather than the predicted cold one, overturning a long-running picture of cosmic fate
It has no effect on it — the long-run future of the universe is entirely independent of the present expansion history, and depends only on initial conditions at the Big Bang
It reverses it — accelerating expansion shows that the universe will eventually collapse back to a single point rather than continuing to expand forever as the old models claimed
questions.context: The heat death has been a philosophical preoccupation since Helmholtz and Kelvin in the mid-1800s. Modern estimates put the era of stellar formation ending around 10^14 years from now and the era of black hole evaporation extending to 10^100 years or more. The long-run picture is not a comfort, but it is one of cosmology's most robust predictions.

questions.question: Ludwig Boltzmann's grave in Vienna's Central Cemetery carries his statistical-mechanical equation as his epitaph: S = k log W. The equation relates the entropy of a macrostate to the number of microstates compatible with it. Why was Boltzmann's contribution received so badly during his life that he died by suicide in 1906?
questions.answer: Many contemporaries — including physicists Mach and Ostwald — denied that atoms even existed, and Boltzmann's statistical mechanics depended on real atoms for its foundation
choices: Many contemporaries — including physicists Mach and Ostwald — denied that atoms even existed, and Boltzmann's statistical mechanics depended on real atoms for its foundation
His equation was mathematically inconsistent — and was later corrected by his student Schrödinger, who eventually published the corrected version under his own name in 1926
Personal scandals had alienated him — from the Austrian academic community, and prevented him from publishing his major work during the most productive period of his career
He was charged with treason — during the First World War and could not work for several years, eventually returning to physics only late in life and never fully recovering
questions.context: Atoms were inferred well before they were directly observed. Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion provided strong evidence for atoms by showing that pollen-grain jitters could be calculated from molecular collisions. Jean Perrin's 1908 experiments completed the case. Boltzmann took his own life shortly before this vindication. His epitaph carries the equation in the form Planck wrote it; Boltzmann never wrote 'k' as a separate constant.

questions.question: All fundamental physical laws — Newton's, Maxwell's, Einstein's, Schrödinger's — work equally well forward and backward in time. Yet we never see broken eggs reassemble themselves. The mismatch is called the 'arrow of time' problem. What's the standard physicist's account?
questions.answer: The arrow comes from initial conditions — the early universe was in an extraordinarily low-entropy state, and the second law's macroscopic asymmetry follows from that starting point
choices: The arrow comes from initial conditions — the early universe was in an extraordinarily low-entropy state, and the second law's macroscopic asymmetry follows from that starting point
The arrow comes from hidden time-asymmetry — buried inside the laws themselves, discovered by Feynman in his 1965 lectures and refined in many subsequent textbook treatments
The arrow is an illusion of human psychology — when examined carefully, it has no physical content at all, and the impression of one-way time comes only from memory limits
The arrow comes from quantum measurement — and disappears entirely in classical systems where there are no observers performing measurements on the system at all
questions.context: Why the universe started in a low-entropy state is a deeper question — Roger Penrose has emphasized that the Big Bang's initial conditions are remarkably special. Possible answers range from anthropic selection (we exist because the entropy was low) to inflation-driven mechanisms to multiverse selection. None is settled. The puzzle is one of cosmology's deepest open questions.

questions.question: Olbers's paradox, named after 19th-century German astronomer Heinrich Olbers but described earlier by Kepler and others, asks: if the universe is infinite and filled with stars, why is the night sky dark? Every line of sight should end on a star, making the sky as bright as the surface of the Sun. What's the resolution?
questions.answer: The observable universe has a finite age — light from very distant stars has not had time to reach us, and the cosmic expansion redshifts what does arrive into low-energy photons we cannot see
choices: The observable universe has a finite age — light from very distant stars has not had time to reach us, and the cosmic expansion redshifts what does arrive into low-energy photons we cannot see
Interstellar dust absorbs all distant starlight — it stops the light before it ever reaches Earth's surface, so distant stars contribute essentially nothing to the brightness of the night sky
The universe is infinite but contains few stars — only a few hundred billion across all of space, far below the number that would be required to brighten our night sky
The night sky is in fact extremely bright — as bright as the surface of the Sun, but human eyes cannot detect light at those wavelengths even when it floods the open sky overhead
questions.context: The dust answer Olbers proposed doesn't work — heated dust would itself radiate. Edgar Allan Poe, of all people, gave a remarkably correct answer in *Eureka* (1848): the universe must be young enough that light from the most distant stars hasn't reached us. Modern cosmology adds the expansion, which redshifts distant light into the microwave background. The dark night sky is itself evidence for a finite-age universe.

questions.question: Russian physicist Pavel Cherenkov observed in 1934 that radioactive substances immersed in clear liquid produced a faint blue glow. The effect was theoretically explained by Igor Tamm and Ilya Frank in 1937. What was Cherenkov's blue light?
questions.answer: Radiation emitted when charged particles travel through a medium — faster than light moves in that same medium, which is analogous to a sonic boom but for light rather than sound
choices: Radiation emitted when charged particles travel through a medium — faster than light moves in that same medium, which is analogous to a sonic boom but for light rather than sound
Radiation produced by chemical reactions — between radioactive elements and the surrounding clear liquid, an unusual combination that does not occur in solid materials at all
Radiation emitted only by uranium isotopes — and not by any other radioactive substances examined since the 1934 discovery, despite many decades of attempts to find a wider class
Radiation that ceased to be observable above 4 kelvin — and could not be reproduced at higher temperatures despite extensive efforts to do so in laboratories across multiple countries
questions.context: Charged particles can exceed the speed of light in a medium (such as water, where light moves at about 75% of vacuum c) without violating relativity — the limit is vacuum c, not c-in-medium. Cherenkov, Tamm, and Frank shared the 1958 Nobel Prize. The effect is used in neutrino detectors like Super-Kamiokande and IceCube: passing neutrinos produce charged particles that emit Cherenkov light, which can be photographed.

questions.question: Superconductivity — the complete vanishing of electrical resistance below a critical temperature — was discovered by Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911. Conventional superconductors (BCS theory 1957) are well understood. But high-temperature superconductors, discovered in 1986 in copper-oxide ceramics by Bednorz and Müller, remain something different. What's the state of that field today?
questions.answer: No agreed mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity — many theoretical proposals exist, but after 40 years no theory has captured a consensus among working condensed-matter physicists
choices: No agreed mechanism for high-temperature superconductivity — many theoretical proposals exist, but after 40 years no theory has captured a consensus among working condensed-matter physicists
Fully explained by an extension of BCS theory — completed by collaborative work in 1993 and refined through the late 1990s, so it is no longer a research topic for the field
Refuted as an experimental artifact — no real materials have ever exhibited the effect at higher temperatures, and the 1986 claims were later traced to instrumentation error
A universal property of every known material — requiring no special mechanism to explain because every substance is superconducting in the right temperature window or pressure regime
questions.context: Bednorz and Müller won the 1987 Nobel Prize (the year after their discovery — the fastest Nobel in physics history). Conventional superconductivity arises from phonon-mediated electron pairing. The high-Tc cuprates appear to involve something else — possibly antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations — but a complete theory has eluded the field. Room-temperature superconductivity at ambient pressure remains a holy grail.

questions.question: Following Aspect's 1982 experiments, decades of work went into closing remaining 'loopholes' in Bell-inequality tests — circumstances under which a local-hidden-variables theorist could still claim the results didn't rule them out. By 2015, three independent groups (Hensen at Delft, Shalm at NIST, Giustina in Vienna) ran 'loophole-free' Bell tests. What did they find?
questions.answer: Violations of Bell inequalities consistent with quantum mechanics — with locality, detection-efficiency, and freedom-of-choice loopholes all closed simultaneously in carefully designed experiments
choices: Violations of Bell inequalities consistent with quantum mechanics — with locality, detection-efficiency, and freedom-of-choice loopholes all closed simultaneously in carefully designed experiments
Confirmation of local hidden variables — and once all the major loopholes were finally closed, the principles of quantum mechanics were refuted at last by clear and decisive measurements
Inconclusive results across all three experiments — the measurements turned out to be too noisy to distinguish between quantum mechanics and any well-formulated local-hidden-variable theory at all
A retraction of Bell's theorem itself — the inequality was found to have been derived incorrectly back in 1964 by Bell, and was formally withdrawn from the literature in 2015
questions.context: The Delft experiment was particularly elegant: two electrons in separate nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamonds 1.3 kilometers apart, entangled through a heralded photon-emission scheme. The loophole-free results closed a half-century of attempts by hidden-variables theorists to find alternative explanations. Whatever quantum entanglement is, it isn't ordinary local correlation.

questions.question: In 1957 Princeton graduate student Hugh Everett III submitted a doctoral thesis proposing a radical interpretation of quantum mechanics: the apparent 'collapse' of the wavefunction is an illusion — instead, each measurement causes the universe to branch into multiple non-interacting copies, one for each possible outcome. What happened to Everett's career?
questions.answer: He was ignored by his Copenhagen-influenced colleagues — left academic physics for defense and consulting work, and his interpretation was revived only in the 1970s by Bryce DeWitt's *Physics Today* article
choices: He was ignored by his Copenhagen-influenced colleagues — left academic physics for defense and consulting work, and his interpretation was revived only in the 1970s by Bryce DeWitt's *Physics Today* article
He won the Nobel Prize in 1959 — and his Many-Worlds interpretation has been the standard textbook interpretation of quantum mechanics ever since, with broad agreement across the field as a whole
He retracted the interpretation in 1972 — and Many-Worlds is no longer considered a serious view by any professional physicist working in the foundations of quantum theory today anywhere
He never published the thesis at all — and Many-Worlds is now associated only with science-fiction writers and popular books rather than with any actual serious foundational physics work
questions.context: Everett's thesis advisor John Wheeler tried to publicize the interpretation, but Niels Bohr's institute received it coldly. Everett moved into the defense industry and apparently never returned to academic physics. Bryce DeWitt's 1970 *Physics Today* article popularized the 'Many-Worlds' label. Today the interpretation has serious advocates (David Deutsch, Sean Carroll, Max Tegmark) — it's not a fringe view, though it remains minority.

questions.question: The 'measurement problem' in quantum mechanics asks: when does the wavefunction stop being a smooth deterministic evolution and become a probabilistic outcome — that is, when does measurement happen? Where exactly does the cut between quantum world and classical world fall?
questions.answer: There is no agreed answer — interpretations place the cut at different points (the apparatus, the observer's mind, never at all), and no experiment has decided between them so far
choices: There is no agreed answer — interpretations place the cut at different points (the apparatus, the observer's mind, never at all), and no experiment has decided between them so far
The cut falls at exactly 10^-23 meters — uniform across all serious interpretations of quantum mechanics, and has been measured directly in tabletop experiments since 2010
The cut was resolved by decoherence theory in 1995 — the measurement problem is no longer considered open by any physicist working in the foundations of quantum mechanics today
The cut falls only inside the human brain — quantum effects vanish precisely at the synapse and not before, in a position widely accepted across the field of neurophysics
questions.context: Copenhagen says measurement collapses the wavefunction (but doesn't say what counts as measurement). Many-Worlds says there is no collapse — observers branch with outcomes. Bohmian mechanics says particles always have definite positions, hidden by stochastic-looking variables. Decoherence (Zeh, Zurek) explains why measurements appear classical but doesn't by itself resolve the 'pick one outcome' question. The cut remains contested.

questions.question: Australian philosopher David Chalmers introduced the term 'hard problem of consciousness' in a 1995 paper. He distinguished it from the 'easy problems' — explaining attention, learning, memory, behavior selection — which neuroscience makes steady progress on. What's the hard problem?
questions.answer: Why any physical process is accompanied by subjective experience — why there's 'something it is like' to be the brain doing those things, rather than just unconscious computation as default
choices: Why any physical process is accompanied by subjective experience — why there's 'something it is like' to be the brain doing those things, rather than just unconscious computation as default
Why neurons fire at certain rates rather than at others — a question that depends on ion-channel gating dynamics and the timing of action-potential propagation across cell membranes
Why humans report having experiences but other primates apparently do not — a comparative question about reports rather than about the underlying nature of subjective experience itself
Why brain imaging requires expensive equipment — and cannot yet be done with simple optical methods at home or in low-resource settings outside of major research hospital facilities
questions.context: Chalmers's example: a perfect physical description of seeing red — wavelengths, retinal cells, optic-nerve signals, V4 activations — seems to leave out the redness, the felt experience. Critics like Daniel Dennett deny the hard problem is a genuine problem. Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, panpsychism, illusionism are competing serious frameworks. None has decisive empirical traction.

questions.question: Francis Crick — yes, the same Crick of DNA fame — turned to consciousness research in the 1980s and worked with Christof Koch for two decades on what they called the 'neural correlates of consciousness': finding the specific brain activity that accompanies conscious awareness. What's the honest summary of progress?
questions.answer: Specific brain regions and patterns correlate with reported conscious experience — but correlation isn't explanation, and the hard problem (why these correlates produce experience) remains entirely untouched
choices: Specific brain regions and patterns correlate with reported conscious experience — but correlation isn't explanation, and the hard problem (why these correlates produce experience) remains entirely untouched
Consciousness was localized to a single brain region — the claustrum, in a definitive 2014 experiment by Koch's group, fully solving the problem to widespread satisfaction in neuroscience
Consciousness has no neural correlates of any kind — as conclusively shown by Tononi's experimental work at the University of Wisconsin in 2008, refuting all neural-correlate research
Consciousness was reduced to specific patterns of electromagnetic radiation — outside the brain entirely, by McFadden's 2002 proposal, which now serves as the field's working consensus
questions.context: Crick and Koch's 1990 paper proposed the claustrum as a possible 'binding' region. Brain imaging has identified default-mode networks, fronto-parietal networks, and other consciousness-linked patterns. Anil Seth, Stanislas Dehaene, and others have done careful work on the global-workspace framework. But Chalmers's challenge — why any of this neural activity should feel like anything — remains as much a philosophical question as a scientific one.

questions.question: Roger Penrose (Nobel laureate in physics 2020) and anesthesiologist Stuart Hameroff have proposed since the 1990s that consciousness arises from quantum effects in microtubules inside neurons — a theory called 'Orchestrated Objective Reduction.' What's the state of this proposal?
questions.answer: Most neuroscientists reject it — quantum effects would decohere too quickly in the warm brain, but a 2024 Mayo Clinic paper detecting microtubule coherence at biological temperatures kept the door slightly open
choices: Most neuroscientists reject it — quantum effects would decohere too quickly in the warm brain, but a 2024 Mayo Clinic paper detecting microtubule coherence at biological temperatures kept the door slightly open
It has been universally accepted — across all of neuroscience and physics since Penrose's 2020 Nobel Prize award, and now serves as the standard textbook model of consciousness
It has been formally refuted — by every experiment ever performed on neural function inside living mammalian brains, leaving no remaining defenders of the original proposal at all today
It is identical to the Global Workspace theory — and is the same proposal under a different name, having been folded into Bernard Baars's framework during the early 2000s
questions.context: Max Tegmark's 2000 paper estimated decoherence timescales in microtubules at about 10^-13 seconds — far too short for neural relevance. Penrose and Hameroff disputed those estimates. The theory is unusual in being a serious physicist's serious proposal that mainstream neuroscience nonetheless mostly dismisses. Whether you find it plausible, the example illustrates how heterodox proposals from established figures can still be marginalized.

questions.question: Most working scientists assume physicalism: that all real phenomena (including consciousness) are ultimately physical. Some serious philosophers and scientists hold non-physicalist views. Which is the recognition skill for the kid?
questions.answer: Physicalism is a philosophical position, not a scientific finding — it is the working assumption of most laboratories, but competing positions (property dualism, panpsychism, idealism) have credentialed defenders even today
choices: Physicalism is a philosophical position, not a scientific finding — it is the working assumption of most laboratories, but competing positions (property dualism, panpsychism, idealism) have credentialed defenders even today

Physicalism has been definitively proven by neuroscience — and has refuted all forms of dualism since 1980, settling a debate that had run between scientists and philosophers since the time of Descartes
Physicalism is rejected by all neuroscientists — since the discovery of quantum effects in microtubules in 1994, which forced the entire field to abandon a purely physical view of mental phenomena
Physicalism applies only to non-living matter — and biological matter requires a separate set of physical laws, a view widely accepted across both biology departments and philosophy departments today
questions.context: David Chalmers defends a property-dualist position. Galen Strawson and Philip Goff defend panpsychism (consciousness as fundamental). Bernardo Kastrup defends a form of idealism. These are not religious views — they are arguments about what the best description of reality includes. The bank does not pick a winner; it teaches the kid that 'science says consciousness is just neurons' overstates what science has actually shown.

questions.question: The technical term 'qualia' (singular: quale) names the felt qualities of experience — the redness of red, the painfulness of pain, the smell of coffee. The Australian philosopher Frank Jackson posed a thought experiment in 1982. What was 'Mary's Room'?
questions.answer: A neuroscientist raised in a black-and-white room — who knows every physical fact about color vision but has never seen color, and learns something new when she first sees red, suggesting experience exceeds physical facts
choices: A neuroscientist raised in a black-and-white room — who knows every physical fact about color vision but has never seen color, and learns something new when she first sees red, suggesting experience exceeds physical facts

A laboratory in which every wall was painted with non-reflective black paint — used to eliminate stray light during sensitive psychology experiments at the University of Sydney during the 1970s and 1980s
A medical-ethics committee meeting room — at the University of Sydney where Jackson first coined the term qualia in 1982, after long debates with the philosophy department about empiricist methods
A virtual-reality simulator built at MIT — used to test color-perception thresholds in research subjects, and the original setting where Mary's Room was discussed in modern peer-reviewed publications
questions.context: Jackson's 'knowledge argument' was widely discussed as a possible refutation of physicalism. Jackson himself later changed his mind and adopted a representationalist response. Daniel Dennett rejects the argument entirely, claiming Mary already knew what she would experience. The debate has not been resolved — it's a paradigm case where a single thought experiment has shaped decades of philosophical work.

questions.question: Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory (IIT), developed since 2004, attempts to give a mathematical definition of consciousness based on 'integrated information' — measured by a quantity called phi. The theory has critics, including a 2023 open letter signed by 124 researchers. Why did they sign?
questions.answer: They argued IIT was an untested and possibly untestable theory — being marketed as established science while still in the early stages of empirical evaluation, ahead of where it had earned that confidence
choices: They argued IIT was an untested and possibly untestable theory — being marketed as established science while still in the early stages of empirical evaluation, ahead of where it had earned that confidence
They argued IIT had been formally proven false — by experiments at Harvard Medical School in 2021, which directly measured phi values incompatible with the theory's basic predictions
They argued IIT was a religious doctrine — and should not be discussed in scientific journals, a position widely accepted by the philosophy community but disputed by Koch's group at Allen
They argued IIT was a duplicate of Daniel Dennett's earlier work — and lacked any original content beyond renaming the consciousness mechanisms he had already proposed two decades before
questions.context: The 'IIT-as-pseudoscience' open letter (Nature 2023) drew its own pushback — some signatories later retracted their support. The debate is partly about what counts as 'pseudoscience,' partly about how new theoretical frameworks should be evaluated, partly about Tononi's collaborator Christof Koch's public advocacy. Honest summary: IIT is one of several serious frameworks, not a closed case in either direction.

questions.question: In 1961 Eugene Wigner published a thought experiment called 'Wigner's Friend.' A friend in a sealed laboratory measures a quantum system; according to Copenhagen, the system's wavefunction collapses for the friend but not for Wigner outside the lab until he opens the door. What did Wigner think this showed?
questions.answer: Possibly that consciousness plays a special role in measurement — though most modern physicists prefer alternative interpretations (decoherence, Many-Worlds) that don't single out minds as central
choices: Possibly that consciousness plays a special role in measurement — though most modern physicists prefer alternative interpretations (decoherence, Many-Worlds) that don't single out minds as central

That Schrödinger's equation was mathematically inconsistent — and required substantial revision to account for the apparent paradox between the friend's experience and Wigner's own outside observation

That cats and other macroscopic objects cannot exist in quantum superpositions — under any conditions, an absolute boundary that has held up against every laboratory test ever attempted by experimentalists
That two observers always agree on every measurement outcome at every instant — an absolute principle of quantum mechanics that cannot be violated by any conceivable experimental arrangement at all
questions.context: Wigner himself later moved away from a consciousness-causes-collapse position. The thought experiment was extended in 2018 by Frauchiger and Renner into a 'no-go' theorem suggesting that quantum mechanics, applied consistently, leads to contradictions between observers. Whether that's a real contradiction or merely a sign that one of the interpretive assumptions must yield is debated. Wigner's Friend remains a live question, not a settled one.

questions.question: In 1859 Irish physicist John Tyndall, working at the Royal Institution in London, used a brass tube, a heated source, and a thermopile to measure how much heat radiation various gases absorbed. He found that nitrogen and oxygen — the main components of air — let heat through, but carbon dioxide and water vapor blocked it strongly. What did this establish?
questions.answer: The infrared physics underlying the greenhouse effect — certain trace gases warm a planet's surface by absorbing outgoing radiation, a basic mechanism still solid in modern textbooks
choices: The infrared physics underlying the greenhouse effect — certain trace gases warm a planet's surface by absorbing outgoing radiation, a basic mechanism still solid in modern textbooks
That nitrogen is the main warming agent in Earth's atmosphere — a result that has held up against every subsequent measurement and now forms a key part of all modern climate models
That heat is a form of matter (the caloric theory) — and not a form of energy as later physicists came to believe, a result that overturned almost every prior textbook on thermal physics
That radiation cannot pass through any gas — refuting the theory of solar heating altogether and leaving an unresolved puzzle about how the Sun's warmth reaches the Earth's surface at all
questions.context: Tyndall's work followed Joseph Fourier's 1820s observation that Earth's surface temperature was higher than incoming solar radiation alone would produce. Svante Arrhenius extended Tyndall's lab work in 1896 with the first quantitative climate-sensitivity calculation. The basic physics — IR absorption by CO2, H2O, methane — is firm. What is contested is the magnitude of net warming after feedbacks, the rate, and what policy should follow.

questions.question: Steven Koonin, former Undersecretary for Science at the Obama-era Department of Energy and a Caltech physicist, published *Unsettled: What Climate Science Tells Us, What It Doesn't, and Why It Matters* in 2021. What was his central claim?
questions.answer: Climate is warming and humans contribute — but the technical chapters of IPCC reports do NOT support the catastrophist framing of media coverage and the surrounding policy debate today
choices: Climate is warming and humans contribute — but the technical chapters of IPCC reports do NOT support the catastrophist framing of media coverage and the surrounding policy debate today
Climate is not warming at all — and all measurements showing warming are products of urban heat-island effects rather than any real change in the underlying global atmospheric temperature
Climate change is real but is caused entirely by solar variability — with no human contribution at any level, contrary to what every reading of the IPCC reports would naturally support
Climate change has been deliberately fabricated — by every climate scientist working since the 1980s, in a sustained coordinated campaign that no critical-thinking person could possibly believe
questions.context: Koonin's book contrasts what the technical IPCC chapters actually say with what Summary-for-Policymakers documents and press coverage report. He documents misleading framings — for example, the claim that hurricanes are getting worse where the technical reports find low confidence in trends. The book takes a middle position: warming yes, anthropogenic contribution yes, but the catastrophe framing is built on top of the reports, not derived from them.

questions.question: Climate sensitivity is the temperature rise expected if atmospheric carbon dioxide doubles from pre-industrial levels. The IPCC's range as of AR6 (2021) is about 2.5 to 4 degrees Celsius, with a best estimate near 3. Why does this range matter so much for policy?
questions.answer: The economic and human costs differ enormously between low and high ends — 2 degrees of warming may be manageable while 4 degrees may not, so the policy debate lives inside the range itself
choices: The economic and human costs differ enormously between low and high ends — 2 degrees of warming may be manageable while 4 degrees may not, so the policy debate lives inside the range itself
Climate sensitivity has been measured to four decimal places — and has no remaining uncertainty after the 2021 IPCC report, leaving the range only as a historical artifact of older expert reviews
Climate sensitivity is irrelevant to policy — warming will occur regardless of any decisions made by governments, so the spread of plausible values has no implication for how we should act
Climate sensitivity was confirmed to be exactly zero — in a major 2023 study from MIT, and is no longer considered uncertain by any climate scientist working in the major institutions worldwide
questions.context: Climate sensitivity has not narrowed much over four decades of work — the IPCC AR1 (1990) range was 1.5-4.5°C; AR6 narrows it only slightly. Feedbacks (cloud feedback in particular) carry most of the uncertainty. Honest reporting names the range, not just a single point estimate, and acknowledges that the policy implications depend strongly on where in the range the truth lies.

questions.question: Michael Mann, Ray Bradley, and Malcolm Hughes published the 'hockey stick' temperature reconstruction in 1998 and 1999. The graph showed nearly flat temperatures for centuries followed by a sharp rise in the 20th century. The graph was prominently featured in IPCC AR3 (2001). What controversies followed?
questions.answer: Statisticians Stephen McIntyre and Ross McKitrick challenged the methodology — the 2006 Wegman Report supported some criticisms, and the 20th-century rise still stands but the 'flat' historical curve was overstated
choices: Statisticians Stephen McIntyre and Ross McKitrick challenged the methodology — the 2006 Wegman Report supported some criticisms, and the 20th-century rise still stands but the 'flat' historical curve was overstated

The graph was confirmed perfectly by every independent study since 1999 — with no methodological concerns raised by any subsequent reanalysis, and the original reconstruction stood unchallenged through subsequent IPCC reports
The graph was withdrawn by Mann himself in 2003 — and is no longer cited by any branch of climate science of any kind, having been fully replaced by a different reconstruction in modern textbooks
The graph showed temperatures decreasing over time — opposite to popular media reporting at the time of its release, a sharp reversal of the standard climate-change framework taught in schools
questions.context: The Medieval Warm Period (around AD 950-1250) and Little Ice Age (around AD 1300-1850) were known to historians and earlier climatologists but were de-emphasized in the original hockey-stick reconstruction. Subsequent work (PAGES 2k Consortium) supports a somewhat less flat historical baseline. The 20th-century warming is itself well-supported, but the framing of unprecedented-flatness-then-sharp-rise has been moderated.

questions.question: Climate models project future temperature changes by simulating atmospheric and oceanic physics. The IPCC uses ensembles of dozens of models with different parameter choices. By 2024, retrospective comparison of model projections from the 1990s and 2000s against actual observations shows what general pattern?
questions.answer: Most models have run somewhat hot — they predicted more warming than has been observed, with the high-end models running significantly hotter than the actual measured surface-temperature record
choices: Most models have run somewhat hot — they predicted more warming than has been observed, with the high-end models running significantly hotter than the actual measured surface-temperature record
Most models have run cold — they significantly underpredicted observed warming across all scenarios examined to date, requiring substantial upward adjustments of their basic input parameters
Models match observations to four decimal places — without any systematic bias detected in either direction, and the matching has held across all major model intercomparison projects to date
Models cannot be compared to observations — the methods are too different to allow meaningful checking, so no honest assessment of model performance against the actual record is possible
questions.context: The high-end CMIP6 models running hot is now well documented — even mainstream climate institutions like Carbon Brief have acknowledged it. The IPCC AR6 adopted a partial weighting scheme to account for this. The pattern doesn't refute climate change — warming has occurred — but it does undermine high-end catastrophe projections that assumed top-of-range models were as reliable as middle-of-range ones.

questions.question: Specific named climate predictions have included: ice-free Arctic by 2013 (Al Gore 2007), ice-free Arctic by 2018 (US Navy 2014), no snow in the UK 'within a few years' (CRU 2000), Manhattan underwater by 2008 (Hansen 1988 interview). What's the recognition skill for the kid reading new specific predictions today?
questions.answer: Specific deadlines on long-range climate predictions have a documented failure rate — high-confidence catastrophe claims should be checked against the record when their dates arrive, a basic media-literacy practice
choices: Specific deadlines on long-range climate predictions have a documented failure rate — high-confidence catastrophe claims should be checked against the record when their dates arrive, a basic media-literacy practice
Specific predictions in climate science are always correct — because the underlying models are well-validated and have a strong track record of getting both short-term and long-term forecasts right
Specific predictions are made only by activists — and not by working scientists, who refrain from any kind of short-term dated claim about climate trends or specific named consequences anywhere

Specific predictions cannot be checked against reality — because climate is too complex for retrospective verification, so no specific prediction has ever been measured against subsequent observations
questions.context: Climate change is real and warming has occurred. But the gap between confident specific-deadline predictions and what has happened is large enough to matter epistemically. Keeping a list of named predictions and their actual outcomes is a basic media-literacy exercise. The lesson is not 'climate change is fake' but 'specific catastrophe predictions have been overconfident, and reasonable skepticism toward new ones is healthy.'

questions.question: On May 29, 1919, British astronomer Arthur Eddington led an expedition to Príncipe (off West Africa) to photograph a total solar eclipse. Einstein's 1915 general relativity predicted gravity would bend starlight passing near the Sun by about 1.75 arcseconds — Newton's theory predicted half that. What did the result do?
questions.answer: Eddington reported that the measurements favored Einstein over Newton — and *The Times* of London ran a front-page headline making Einstein a worldwide celebrity overnight, more famous than any other living scientist
choices: Eddington reported that the measurements favored Einstein over Newton — and *The Times* of London ran a front-page headline making Einstein a worldwide celebrity overnight, more famous than any other living scientist
Eddington reported the bending equaled Newton's value — and the result was widely interpreted as a refutation of general relativity, leaving Einstein's theory in difficulty for decades after 1919

Eddington found no bending at all in the eclipse photographs — and both theories were considered untested for many years afterwards, with the eclipse expedition treated as inconclusive across the field

Eddington died during the eclipse expedition itself — and the data was never properly analyzed by any other scientist, leaving the 1919 measurements as an unfinished chapter in twentieth-century physics
questions.context: Modern reanalysis of Eddington's plates has questioned how confidently the 1919 data alone could distinguish the two theories. But many later eclipses, radio-telescope measurements of quasars, and the 2018 measurement of an electron's gravitational deflection have confirmed Einstein's prediction with high precision. The 1919 announcement was scientifically borderline but historically decisive.

questions.question: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks. General relativity predicts those clocks tick faster than identical clocks on Earth's surface, because they're in a weaker gravitational field — by about 45 microseconds per day. Special relativity predicts they tick slower by about 7 microseconds per day due to orbital speed. What would happen if relativity weren't corrected for?
questions.answer: GPS position estimates would drift by about 10 kilometers per day — the system would be useless within hours of starting up, since no relativistic correction would be built into the broadcast time signals
choices: GPS position estimates would drift by about 10 kilometers per day — the system would be useless within hours of starting up, since no relativistic correction would be built into the broadcast time signals
GPS position estimates would be slightly less accurate — but still usable for ordinary navigation, with only minor degradation that consumer users would never notice in everyday use
GPS satellites would not function at all — they would lose orbital stability without relativistic corrections to their clocks and tumble out of their orbits within several months
GPS would be unaffected by relativity entirely — relativistic effects cancel out exactly across multiple satellites in formation overhead, leaving broadcast times identical to ground clocks always
questions.context: GPS is one of the most striking practical confirmations of relativity. Both general (gravitational time dilation) and special (kinematic time dilation) effects matter and must be included.
