choices: Peer review checks plausibility and logical coherence — but reviewers rarely see raw data, repeat experiments, or examine code, so it does not reliably catch fraud or replicate findings, and the Surgisphere case proved this

Peer review catches all forms of fraud automatically — this is why the Stapel, Hwang, and Surgisphere cases were caught before publication, and why no fraudulent papers have ever appeared in major journals at all

Peer review is performed by computers using AI — so any fraud is detected algorithmically before the paper reaches reviewers, making fraud in modern science essentially impossible at the top journals worldwide
Peer review involves attempting to replicate every result — so each published study has been independently confirmed at least once before it appears in any major journal, with full open data provided
questions.context: Peer review's actual function is much more limited than the public image suggests. Reviewers are usually given a manuscript, sometimes summary data, and asked to evaluate its presentation, methods, and plausibility — typically over a few hours, often unpaid. They almost never request raw data, repeat experiments, or examine code. Fraud detection is rare. The replication crisis exposed how thin the review process actually is. None of this means peer review is worthless, but it is overrated.

questions.question: Pre-registration is the practice of publicly declaring a study's hypotheses, methods, and analyses BEFORE collecting data. Major journals have increasingly required or encouraged it since around 2015. Why is it considered the strongest defense against the problems Ioannidis identified?
questions.answer: Pre-registration prevents researchers from retrofitting analyses to whatever the data happens to show — separating the prediction stage from the analysis stage and making p-hacking visible in the public record
choices: Pre-registration prevents researchers from retrofitting analyses to whatever the data happens to show — separating the prediction stage from the analysis stage and making p-hacking visible in the public record

Pre-registration eliminates the need for controls — once a study is registered, no further safeguards are required, and the registration itself counts as a guarantee of result reliability under every journal policy

Pre-registration is a marketing tool only — it does not actually affect the reliability of published findings, and was adopted by journals as public-relations response without any statistical justification at all

Pre-registration replaces peer review entirely — modern pre-registered studies are not reviewed before publication, and journals publish them automatically once the registered protocol has been followed by the author
questions.context: Pre-registration distinguishes 'exploratory' research (where you look for patterns) from 'confirmatory' research (where you test specific predictions). Both have value, but they require different epistemic credit. Pre-registered confirmatory studies have shown markedly better replication rates than non-pre-registered work. The Open Science Framework hosts public pre-registrations. Registered Reports (peer-reviewed BEFORE data collection) take the principle further.

questions.question: The 'file drawer problem,' first named by Robert Rosenthal in 1979, refers to a particular kind of selection bias in published science. Negative results — studies that found no effect — tend to stay unpublished in researchers' file drawers. What's the effect on the literature?
questions.answer: The published record overstates how often real effects exist — because only the successes get published while the failed replications and null results stay hidden, distorting any meta-analysis built on the visible record
choices: The published record overstates how often real effects exist — because only the successes get published while the failed replications and null results stay hidden, distorting any meta-analysis built on the visible record

The published record understates how often real effects exist — because journals systematically refuse to publish positive findings, preferring null results that confirm the safety of older established theories

The published record is perfectly representative — because journals adopted automatic submission policies in 2010, eliminating any possibility of bias from researchers' decisions about what to write up

The published record contains only randomly selected studies — because journals use lottery systems to choose which papers to print from those submitted, ensuring representative sampling of the entire field
questions.context: Rosenthal's 'fail-safe N' calculation estimated how many unpublished null results would be needed to overturn a meta-analytic conclusion. Modern responses include results-blind review (judging studies on methods before data), the registered reports format, and journals dedicated to null and negative findings. Trial-registration requirements in clinical research (since around 2005 under FDA AERS and the WHO ICTRP) were one of the strongest reforms — though compliance remains imperfect.

questions.question: The 'Many Labs' replication projects, beginning in 2014, are coordinated efforts in which dozens of independent laboratories simultaneously attempt to replicate the same set of well-known psychology findings. The advantage over single-lab replications is methodological. What is it?
questions.answer: Multi-lab effort statistically distinguishes failures due to subtle context from genuine non-replication — and produces high-quality estimates of effect sizes much more reliable than any single study could yield
choices: Multi-lab effort statistically distinguishes failures due to subtle context from genuine non-replication — and produces high-quality estimates of effect sizes much more reliable than any single study could yield

Multi-lab effort is required by every major journal — single-lab studies have been banned since 2017 in psychology and biomedical research, with no exceptions allowed under any current publication standard

Multi-lab effort uses larger statistical software packages — eliminating computational errors that contaminate single-lab studies, even though the underlying experimental methodology remains identical across labs

Multi-lab effort is cheaper than single-lab replication — costs drop dramatically once 30 labs participate, even though the total person-hours required scale linearly with the number of participating sites involved
questions.context: Many Labs 1 (2014, ~6,000 participants) replicated 10 of 13 effects. Many Labs 2 (2018) replicated about 14 of 28. The classic Stanford prison experiment, ego depletion, and power-pose effect all failed to replicate in Many Labs settings. The collaborative-replication framework is one of the strongest reforms to come out of the crisis — it makes both successes and failures more interpretable than single-lab work.

questions.question: Congress passed the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act in 1986, creating the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program and shielding manufacturers from most lawsuits over childhood vaccine injuries. The CDC schedule has grown from about 11 doses by age 6 in 1986 to 70+ doses by age 18 today. What structural concern do critics name?
questions.answer: Removing manufacturer liability changes incentives — companies cannot be sued the way other drug makers can, which weakens the market discipline that ordinarily forces safer products on the market
choices: Removing manufacturer liability changes incentives — companies cannot be sued the way other drug makers can, which weakens the market discipline that ordinarily forces safer products on the market
Vaccines were declared exempt from medical-ethics review — Congress in 1986 ended all oversight of vaccine safety, leaving no federal or state regulatory authority to review childhood vaccines today

The 1986 law made vaccines free for all children — regardless of income or insurance coverage, removing a financial barrier that had previously prevented widespread immunization in many parts of the country

The 1986 law specifically banned any future research — into vaccine safety questions, leaving the field unable to investigate any concerns raised by parents or by independent doctors over the past decades
questions.context: Pre-1986 vaccine-injury lawsuits had threatened manufacturer participation in the childhood vaccine market. The 1986 NCVIA shielded manufacturers, created VICP as a no-fault compensation system, and routed claims through a federal claims court. Critics including Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and attorney Aaron Siri argue the liability shield combined with mandate pressure weakens the normal market discipline of liability litigation. The schedule expansion is documented in CDC's published childhood immunization schedules.

questions.question: The Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) is the main federal database for reports of possible vaccine injuries. A 2010 Harvard Pilgrim Health Care study estimated VAERS captures less than 1% of all vaccine adverse events. What does this mean for interpreting VAERS data?
questions.answer: VAERS shows reports submitted — not all actual events, so it cannot directly estimate true injury rates, but a 1% capture rate also means observed signals likely represent much larger underlying problems
choices: VAERS shows reports submitted — not all actual events, so it cannot directly estimate true injury rates, but a 1% capture rate also means observed signals likely represent much larger underlying problems
VAERS captures every adverse event — and is the gold standard for vaccine safety surveillance, with no other system needed to verify the safety profile of any childhood vaccine on the schedule

VAERS captures only the most severe reactions — and so its numbers should be multiplied by ten thousand to get accurate population figures, regardless of any concerns about reporter behavior or selection bias

VAERS was discontinued in 2015 — and no current data is available for any vaccine introduced since then, leaving the post-2015 safety profile of childhood vaccines essentially undocumented at the federal level
questions.context: The 2010 Harvard Pilgrim study (Lazarus et al.) was contracted by HHS to evaluate VAERS. Its conclusion that VAERS captures <1% of events was published but not aggressively followed up by federal agencies. VAERS is by design a passive surveillance system — anyone can submit, but most events are never reported. Critics argue this asymmetry is a structural problem: the same federal agencies that promote vaccination also run the main safety database. The recognition skill is reading 'VAERS shows X' carefully.

questions.question: The CDC childhood vaccine schedule has expanded substantially over four decades. In 1986, children received about 11 doses by age 6. By 2024, children are recommended to receive 70+ doses by age 18 across roughly 16 different vaccines. What's the recognition skill?
questions.answer: Schedule expansion reflects multiple factors — new diseases targeted, new combination vaccines, new doses added to existing series — and the long-term safety profile of receiving so many vaccines together is much less studied than individual-vaccine effects
choices: Schedule expansion reflects multiple factors — new diseases targeted, new combination vaccines, new doses added to existing series — and the long-term safety profile of receiving so many vaccines together is much less studied than individual-vaccine effects

Schedule expansion reflects single-disease additions only — each new vaccine is added based on a randomized controlled trial of the schedule as a whole, so combined safety is exhaustively studied before approval

Schedule expansion has not actually occurred — the current childhood schedule contains the same vaccines as the 1986 schedule, and reports of additional doses are based on incorrect or out-of-date documents

Schedule expansion reflects exclusively private-industry decisions — the CDC plays no role in determining which vaccines are added or recommended, leaving the schedule purely to insurance industry preferences
questions.context: Each individual vaccine has typically been tested before licensing, but the question of cumulative interaction across the schedule is less well-studied. A randomized trial comparing the full schedule against any alternative would be considered unethical (it would require withholding vaccines). Observational studies face significant confounding. RFK Jr. and others have made the 'no placebo-controlled schedule trial' point as a structural critique that the science deserves better than dismissal.

questions.question: In 1998 British gastroenterologist Andrew Wakefield published a 12-patient case series in *The Lancet* suggesting a possible link between the MMR vaccine and autism. The paper was fully retracted in 2010 after journalist Brian Deer documented serious methodological and ethical problems. What had Deer found?
questions.answer: Undisclosed financial conflicts of interest — alterations to patient case histories, and procedures performed on children without proper ethical approval, combining to make the original paper unreliable
choices: Undisclosed financial conflicts of interest — alterations to patient case histories, and procedures performed on children without proper ethical approval, combining to make the original paper unreliable

Pure laboratory error in the original data — but no ethical concerns, with Wakefield himself recommending the retraction once the technical errors were brought to his attention by independent reviewers

Strong evidence that MMR caused autism — but the medical establishment forced retraction for political reasons, with no actual methodological or ethical concerns regarding the original 12-patient study itself

Plagiarism of an earlier German study — that had reached the same conclusions about MMR and autism, with Wakefield acknowledged as the original source by the underlying German research team in private
questions.context: The Wakefield episode is genuinely complex. The 1998 paper itself was small (12 children), made cautious claims, and called for further investigation. Wakefield was struck off the UK medical register in 2010. Some critics have argued the deregistration was disproportionate or politically driven. The retraction itself is settled. The broader politics of the MMR controversy, parental concerns about autism, and the relationship between scientific dissent and professional sanction remain contested. The bank covers this honestly.

questions.question: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., environmental lawyer and founder of Children's Health Defense, has been the most prominent US public figure questioning current vaccine policy for over two decades. He served as US Secretary of Health and Human Services from 2025. What's his substantive position on vaccines?
questions.answer: Kennedy supports placebo-controlled safety testing — challenges the manufacturer liability shield, and has called for independent reviews of the schedule rather than the 'anti-vaccine' label often used to dismiss him
choices: Kennedy supports placebo-controlled safety testing — challenges the manufacturer liability shield, and has called for independent reviews of the schedule rather than the 'anti-vaccine' label often used to dismiss him
Kennedy believes all vaccines are entirely safe — and has called for expanding the CDC schedule to add more required doses, a position he has held consistently throughout his career
Kennedy believes all diseases are caused by vaccines — and has called for banning every vaccine on the schedule, a position he has held without modification since at least the year 2005
Kennedy was elected President of the United States in 2024 — and his vaccine policies became the official position of the federal government during his first term in the White House
questions.context: Kennedy's positions evolved over time and resist the absolutist labels often applied to them. He has supported informed consent, placebo-controlled safety testing, repeal of the 1986 liability shield, and independent review of childhood-vaccine schedules. He has explicitly disclaimed being 'anti-vaccine' and supports the smallpox eradication. He was nominated and confirmed as HHS Secretary in early 2025. The recognition skill: 'anti-vaxxer' is a label used to dismiss substantive policy disagreement, not a description of the actual position.

questions.question: The Great Barrington Declaration, published October 2020, was drafted by Jay Bhattacharya (Stanford), Martin Kulldorff (Harvard), and Sunetra Gupta (Oxford). It called for focused protection of the vulnerable rather than population-wide lockdowns. NIH director Francis Collins privately called for 'a quick and devastating takedown.' How did this resolve?
questions.answer: Bhattacharya was confirmed as NIH director under Trump in 2025 — vindicating the GBD signatories on the institutional stage, and the Collins emails were released through House Judiciary FOIA
choices: Bhattacharya was confirmed as NIH director under Trump in 2025 — vindicating the GBD signatories on the institutional stage, and the Collins emails were released through House Judiciary FOIA
The signatories were retracted by their universities — and the Declaration was formally withdrawn within weeks of publication, with no remaining defenders by 2021 in mainstream academic medicine

Collins was promoted to head of WHO — and the Great Barrington Declaration was added to a federal list of misinformation, with all three signatories formally censured by professional societies in 2021

The signatories signed a public retraction — apologizing for their original views and acknowledging Collins's framework as scientifically correct, with no remaining defenders by 2022 in mainstream science
questions.context: Jay Bhattacharya (Stanford), Martin Kulldorff (Harvard), and Sunetra Gupta (Oxford) drafted the Declaration at the American Institute for Economic Research. FOIA-released emails (House Judiciary 2023) showed Collins emailing Anthony Fauci about the 'quick and devastating takedown' on October 8, 2020. Bhattacharya was confirmed as NIH director under the Trump administration in 2025. The recognition skill: credentialed scientific dissenters can be marginalized at the institutional level and later vindicated when political winds shift.

questions.question: The Cochrane Collaboration is widely regarded as the gold standard for evidence-based medicine reviews. Its 2023 update on physical interventions to interrupt respiratory virus spread examined randomized controlled trials of mask use. What did the review conclude?
questions.answer: Wearing masks in the community probably makes little or no difference to the spread of respiratory viruses — based on randomized trial evidence, though Cochrane's editor later issued a public statement softening the conclusion under political pressure
choices: Wearing masks in the community probably makes little or no difference to the spread of respiratory viruses — based on randomized trial evidence, though Cochrane's editor later issued a public statement softening the conclusion under political pressure

Mask mandates definitively prevent all respiratory infections — based on randomized trial evidence, in a sweeping finding that supports the COVID-era mandate policies imposed by most US states across the country

The review was retracted before publication — and Cochrane has not yet issued any opinion on the question of whether community mask use reduces respiratory virus transmission in randomized trial settings

The review found inconclusive results in all directions — and Cochrane recommended that the question be left to individual state and local health officials to determine based on their own preferences and politics
questions.context: The Cochrane mask review (Jefferson et al. 2023) was an update to a long-standing review. Its primary finding was that randomized evidence did NOT support strong claims about community mask effectiveness against respiratory viruses. Cochrane's editor-in-chief Karla Soares-Weiser later issued a clarifying statement that has itself been criticized as walking back the review's actual conclusions. The episode illustrates how political pressure shapes how even gold-standard reviews are presented to the public.

questions.question: Martin Kulldorff was a biostatistician at Harvard Medical School, where he co-developed the standard surveillance methodology US public health authorities use to detect disease outbreaks. He was removed from key vaccine-safety advisory roles after signing the Great Barrington Declaration. What's the recognition skill?
questions.answer: A leading expert on outbreak detection — using his own published method, was removed from advisory roles for publicly disagreeing with the lockdown framework, illustrating how dissent could result in institutional sanction
choices: A leading expert on outbreak detection — using his own published method, was removed from advisory roles for publicly disagreeing with the lockdown framework, illustrating how dissent could result in institutional sanction

Kulldorff was a low-ranked researcher — with no significant publications, and his removal from advisory roles reflected the normal academic turnover process rather than any reaction to his public positions
Kulldorff was rewarded with promotions — for signing the Great Barrington Declaration, and Harvard expanded his responsibilities throughout 2021 in recognition of his contributions to public health

Kulldorff did not actually sign the Declaration — and the entire incident is a fabrication, with no documented dispute between him and any institutional employer in any year since the start of his career
questions.context: Kulldorff developed the SaTScan space-time scan statistic widely used in disease-surveillance work. He served on the FDA's Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee and the CDC's ACIP Vaccine Safety Subgroup. After the GBD, he was removed from the ACIP subgroup and lost his Harvard position. The case is one of the cleanest examples of how publicly questioning policy during COVID could result in professional consequences even for credentialed researchers.

questions.question: Peter McCullough is a cardiologist who chaired the COVID treatment guidance committee for the Truth for Health Foundation and published over 50 COVID-related papers — many on early-treatment protocols. The American Board of Internal Medicine moved to revoke his certifications. What does this illustrate?
questions.answer: Professional boards moved to discipline dissenting physicians — using vague 'misinformation' charges, even when the dissent involved protocols McCullough himself had studied in published cardiology research
choices: Professional boards moved to discipline dissenting physicians — using vague 'misinformation' charges, even when the dissent involved protocols McCullough himself had studied in published cardiology research

Professional boards revoke certifications only for criminal fraud — so any discipline imposed on McCullough must have been for serious patient harm, regardless of his stated reasons in any public defense

Professional boards have no actual authority over physician certifications — and McCullough remained certified throughout the pandemic with no actions taken by any board in response to his various statements
Professional boards endorsed all of McCullough's positions — promoting him as a leading voice in COVID care, and expanding his certifications during the pandemic in recognition of his contributions
questions.context: The ABIM and Texas Medical Board both moved against McCullough. Similar actions affected Pierre Kory, Ryan Cole, and other dissenting physicians. The legal questions remain ongoing — some board actions have been challenged in court, and several have been blocked or reversed. The pattern is a generalizable one: professional certifying organizations gained new power during COVID to discipline dissent on policy questions framed as 'misinformation,' and have been slow to update as the underlying claims have been re-evaluated.

questions.question: The WHO Smallpox Eradication Program ran from 1967 to 1980. Smallpox had killed roughly 300 million people in the 20th century alone. The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin in Somalia, October 1977. WHO formally declared eradication May 8, 1980. What does this episode genuinely show?
questions.answer: A vaccine-based public health program eradicated a major killer of humanity — and stands as one of the great achievements of biomedical science, distinct from the contested questions about specific modern vaccines and policy frameworks
choices: A vaccine-based public health program eradicated a major killer of humanity — and stands as one of the great achievements of biomedical science, distinct from the contested questions about specific modern vaccines and policy frameworks
All vaccines are universally effective — and the smallpox case proves there is no legitimate ground for any criticism of any vaccine that has appeared on any childhood schedule at any time anywhere
No vaccine has ever been effective — and the smallpox 'eradication' is a fabrication, with the disease still circulating widely in undeveloped countries despite WHO claims to the contrary about 1980

Public health programs always work — and there are no contested cases worth examining anywhere in the history of biomedical or public-health research over the past century of organized vaccination effort
questions.context: Smallpox eradication is biomedical science at its best — a hard problem solved with a real vaccine. It deserves recognition without being weaponized to silence questions about other vaccines or other policies. The bank covers it honestly. The variola virus exists only in two known secured laboratories. Eradication is the only example for any infectious disease; polio eradication has been close for decades but has not succeeded. The recognition skill: distinguishing legitimate triumphs from specific contested cases is part of mature thinking on the topic.

questions.question: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren published their *Helicobacter pylori* hypothesis in *The Lancet* in 1984. They argued the bacterium caused stomach ulcers — overturning decades of teaching that ulcers came from stress, spicy food, and excess acid. They won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Medicine. What's the broader recognition skill?
questions.answer: Scientific consensus can be wrong for decades — Marshall's case is the textbook example of how an outsider's careful work can overturn established teaching, with similar reversals throughout medical history
choices: Scientific consensus can be wrong for decades — Marshall's case is the textbook example of how an outsider's careful work can overturn established teaching, with similar reversals throughout medical history

Scientific consensus is always correct — Marshall's case is the only known exception in the modern era, so the consensus on any current issue should always be accepted regardless of any contrary evidence

Scientific outsiders are always right — Marshall's case proves every dissenter eventually wins, so any current dissenter should be granted the benefit of the doubt regardless of the actual evidence presented

Scientific consensus changes only through formal vote — and Marshall's case was settled when the Nobel committee voted for him in 2005, after which the previous consensus position was formally withdrawn
questions.context: Marshall famously drank a beaker of *H. pylori* in 1984 after no one would replicate his work, developed gastritis within days, and cured himself with antibiotics. The medical mainstream had ridiculed the idea that any bacterium could survive stomach acid. Now ulcers are routinely cured with antibiotics. The case is one of medicine's clearest examples of consensus being wrong. The skill is recognizing that 'consensus' is not a synonym for truth and 'outsider' is not a synonym for fringe.

questions.question: In 1847, Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors washing hands with chlorinated lime cut maternity-ward deaths from about 18% to about 1%. The medical establishment rejected his work; he was institutionalized and died in an asylum in 1865. Why did the establishment reject such a clear statistical case?
questions.answer: Semmelweis could not explain WHY hand-washing worked — germ theory came decades later from Pasteur and Koch, and without a mechanism, his statistical evidence was rejected by physicians who saw his data as inexplicable
choices: Semmelweis could not explain WHY hand-washing worked — germ theory came decades later from Pasteur and Koch, and without a mechanism, his statistical evidence was rejected by physicians who saw his data as inexplicable
Semmelweis had falsified his data — and the establishment correctly rejected his work after a careful examination of his actual case records by an independent committee of senior practitioners

Semmelweis was uneducated and unqualified — without a medical degree of any kind, so his evidence carried no weight in any professional setting and was correctly dismissed by his contemporaries in Vienna

Semmelweis was politically subversive — and his work was suppressed by the Habsburg authorities under explicit imperial orders, not because of any genuine scientific disagreement about the underlying claim
questions.context: Semmelweis's case has become emblematic. He had data that should have changed practice — and physicians rejected it because it lacked a mechanism and because admitting it would have meant admitting that doctors had been killing their own patients. Lister extended his work to surgical antisepsis. Semmelweis died in 1865 — possibly from sepsis after being beaten by asylum guards. He was vindicated only posthumously. The recognition skill: 'no mechanism' is not the same as 'no effect.'

questions.question: Although Wegener's continental drift is classically a geology story, his case illustrates a recurring pattern in biology too. The 'native intellect' of established fields is to reject explanations from outside their discipline. What's an example from biology where this happened?
questions.answer: Lynn Margulis's endosymbiotic theory of cell organelles — mitochondria and chloroplasts as descendants of free-living bacteria — was rejected for over a decade after her 1967 paper, then vindicated by genetic evidence
choices: Lynn Margulis's endosymbiotic theory of cell organelles — mitochondria and chloroplasts as descendants of free-living bacteria — was rejected for over a decade after her 1967 paper, then vindicated by genetic evidence

Watson and Crick's DNA helix model — was rejected for over a decade after their 1953 paper, and was eventually accepted only after Rosalind Franklin published her own independent confirmation of the basic helix shape

Linnaeus's classification system — was rejected for over a century after his 1735 publication, and was eventually accepted only when the genetic basis for species differences became clear through modern DNA sequencing

Pasteur's germ theory — was rejected for over a century in mainstream biology, and was eventually accepted only after the discovery of antibiotics had eliminated bacteria from the surrounding clinical environment
questions.context: Lynn Margulis's 'On the origin of mitosing cells' (1967) was rejected by 15 journals before publication. She argued mitochondria and chloroplasts had originated as free-living bacteria that took up residence inside other cells. The mainstream considered the idea wild. Sequence evidence in the 1980s showed mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA were unambiguously bacterial in origin. Margulis (1938-2011) was vindicated. She was a difficult colleague but profoundly correct on the central point.

questions.question: After Marshall and Warren's *H. pylori* discovery was accepted, the treatment of peptic ulcers changed almost overnight. What's the most striking statistic about this transition?
questions.answer: Ulcer-related surgeries dropped by more than 80% within a decade — as antibiotics replaced surgery, and the H2-blocker and proton-pump-inhibitor pharmaceutical markets shrank dramatically over the following years
choices: Ulcer-related surgeries dropped by more than 80% within a decade — as antibiotics replaced surgery, and the H2-blocker and proton-pump-inhibitor pharmaceutical markets shrank dramatically over the following years

Ulcer-related surgeries stayed exactly the same — for the following two decades, even after Marshall's work was widely accepted, because hospital surgical departments had no incentive to change their established practices

Ulcer-related surgeries doubled within five years — as patients who had been managing with diet now sought surgical intervention combined with antibiotic treatment, the standard care became surgery plus antibiotics

Ulcer-related surgeries were declared unethical — and physicians who continued to perform them were stripped of certification by the American Board of Surgery starting from 1990, regardless of patient request
questions.context: Before *H. pylori* was accepted as causative, peptic ulcers were chronic conditions treated with dietary changes, stomach-acid suppressors, and frequently surgery. After antibiotics were established as curative, surgery rates collapsed. The change is one of the cleanest examples of a basic scientific discovery (a bacterium identified) translating immediately into clinical impact. The H2-blocker industry had been a multi-billion-dollar business; the proton-pump-inhibitor industry continued but for less serious conditions.

questions.question: Alexander Fleming, in his 1945 Nobel Prize acceptance speech, warned that bacterial resistance to penicillin would inevitably evolve if the drug was overused. Resistance has indeed evolved across decades. What's the basic mechanism?
questions.answer: Bacterial populations naturally contain rare resistant variants — and antibiotic use selectively kills the susceptible majority, leaving resistant bacteria to grow into the next generation in greater numbers
choices: Bacterial populations naturally contain rare resistant variants — and antibiotic use selectively kills the susceptible majority, leaving resistant bacteria to grow into the next generation in greater numbers

Bacteria deliberately mutate when threatened — through a directed process that creates exactly the resistance gene needed against whatever antibiotic is being used, in response to a sensed chemical threat

Antibiotic resistance is a genuine myth — created by pharmaceutical companies to sell newer drugs, and there is no evidence that any antibiotic has lost effectiveness against any common bacterial pathogen

Antibiotic resistance occurs only in laboratory settings — in real patients, all bacteria remain susceptible to all antibiotics introduced over the past 80 years, with no documented field cases of treatment failure
questions.context: Bacterial resistance evolution is a textbook example of natural selection in real time. Resistant variants exist by random mutation before any antibiotic exposure; antibiotic use favors them. Horizontal gene transfer between bacteria spreads resistance quickly. Major resistant pathogens — MRSA, multi-drug-resistant TB, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae — are global concerns. The biological mechanism is uncontroversial; what is contested is policy (antibiotic restriction, agricultural use, novel-drug R&D incentives).

questions.question: Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA) emerged in the 1960s, just years after methicillin itself was introduced. By the 1990s and 2000s, MRSA had become a major hospital pathogen and a community pathogen. What's the recognition skill?
questions.answer: The rate of new resistant strains often exceeds the rate of new antibiotic development — and many companies have exited antibiotic R&D entirely, leaving the world with a thinning arsenal against an evolving threat
choices: The rate of new resistant strains often exceeds the rate of new antibiotic development — and many companies have exited antibiotic R&D entirely, leaving the world with a thinning arsenal against an evolving threat

Every resistant strain is matched by a new antibiotic within months — and pharmaceutical companies maintain a 30-strain pipeline of new drugs at all times, with no risk of running out of antibiotics in clinical use anywhere

MRSA was eradicated globally in 2010 — and is no longer a public-health concern, with all hospitals reporting zero cases since the eradication declaration was issued by the World Health Organization the same year

MRSA is an environmental contaminant from soil — and is unrelated to actual antibiotic use in humans, with all the resistance arising independently in soil bacteria rather than from clinical selection pressure
questions.context: Antibiotic R&D is structurally unprofitable for pharmaceutical companies: any new antibiotic is held in reserve to delay resistance, which means low sales volume, which means insufficient return on the development cost. Many large pharma firms have shut down their antibiotic divisions. The result is a real public-health crisis that does not fit standard market incentives. Government push-and-pull initiatives (BARDA, GAIN Act, AMR Action Fund) have had limited success. The recognition skill: market failure is real here.

questions.question: Chemistry had its phlogiston theory — wrong but widely held for over a century. Medicine has had its 'humoral theory' — Hippocrates and Galen's four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) dominated Western medicine for nearly two millennia. What finally killed humoral theory?
questions.answer: Pasteur's germ theory and Koch's postulates in the late 1800s — gave bacteria a documented role in specific diseases, making the four-humors framework unnecessary for explaining illness across the spectrum
choices: Pasteur's germ theory and Koch's postulates in the late 1800s — gave bacteria a documented role in specific diseases, making the four-humors framework unnecessary for explaining illness across the spectrum

The American Medical Association's vote in 1847 — formally banned humoral theory from being taught in any medical school in the United States starting that year, regardless of evidence or supporter arguments
Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis — replaced humoral theory with psychological explanations of illness, and the four-humors framework had no influence on twentieth-century Western medicine in any way
Modern genetics in the early 2000s — provided the first genuine alternative to humoral theory, and Western medicine had been teaching the four humors continuously until that time without dispute
questions.context: Humoral theory survived an astonishing length of time precisely because it was unfalsifiable — virtually any patient's illness could be retrofitted to humor imbalance. Galen's authority lasted from the 2nd century AD through the Renaissance. Bloodletting (correcting 'excess' blood) killed George Washington in 1799 — a relatively modern date. The germ-theory transition wasn't instantaneous; older physicians often continued humoral practice for decades. The recognition skill: even long-held medical doctrines can be wrong.

questions.question: The 'diet-heart hypothesis' — that dietary saturated fat and cholesterol cause heart disease — was the dominant US nutrition policy from the 1970s through the 2010s. Ancel Keys's Seven Countries Study (1960s) became its foundation. By the 2020s, the position had eroded. What's the recognition skill?
questions.answer: Major nutrition policies can rest on weak evidence — and persist for decades through institutional inertia, with the diet-heart framework now widely seen as oversold even within mainstream nutrition science
choices: Major nutrition policies can rest on weak evidence — and persist for decades through institutional inertia, with the diet-heart framework now widely seen as oversold even within mainstream nutrition science

Nutrition science is exact and reliable — and the diet-heart hypothesis remains the firmly established mainstream view, with modern dietary guidelines built on its consensus across every major country

Nutrition policies are revised every five years — based on randomized controlled trials, so the diet-heart hypothesis has been replaced by current guidelines that supersede all previous recommendations
Nutrition science was banned from publication in 2015 — and no current policy is informed by any actual scientific finding, since the field was determined to be too unreliable for any practical use
questions.context: Ancel Keys's Seven Countries Study has been criticized for selection bias (Keys reportedly excluded countries that did not fit his hypothesis). The Minnesota Coronary Experiment (1968-1973) was a randomized trial that failed to show benefit from reducing saturated fat — and was not published for over 40 years. Nina Teicholz's *The Big Fat Surprise* (2014) made the historical case. The current mainstream nutrition view is much more cautious about saturated-fat alarmism than the 1980s version was, though not yet converged.

questions.question: The Cambrian explosion — about 538 million years ago — saw the geologically rapid appearance of nearly all modern animal phyla in the fossil record over perhaps 20 to 25 million years. Charles Darwin himself called this 'inexplicable' in *On the Origin of Species*. What does the modern view look like?
questions.answer: Modern paleontology has many proposed explanations but no decisive one — including oxygen rise, ecosystem dynamics, and gene-toolkit innovations, but the pace of body-plan change remains one of evolution's striking facts
choices: Modern paleontology has many proposed explanations but no decisive one — including oxygen rise, ecosystem dynamics, and gene-toolkit innovations, but the pace of body-plan change remains one of evolution's striking facts

The Cambrian explosion has been definitively explained — by the 1989 discovery of the Burgess Shale formations, with no remaining puzzle about how animal body plans first arose in deep geological time

The Cambrian explosion never actually occurred — and is an artifact of incomplete fossil sampling that disappears once paleontologists examine the full pre-Cambrian record in the major sedimentary basins

The Cambrian explosion was caused by a single asteroid impact — that triggered the first complex life on Earth, in a finding now widely accepted in mainstream paleontology since the 2010 reanalysis efforts
questions.context: The Burgess Shale (1909) and Chengjiang biota (China, 1980s) revealed the extraordinary diversity of Cambrian fauna. Pre-Cambrian life was largely microbial and simple multicellular. The transition to a fauna recognizably modern in basic body plans is genuinely puzzling. Several recent hypotheses converge on multiple contributing factors (oxygen, predation, gene regulation). The bank honors this as one of biology's open questions rather than pretending to a tidy solution.

questions.question: Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould published 'Punctuated Equilibria: An Alternative to Phyletic Gradualism' in 1972. They argued the fossil record shows long periods of stasis punctuated by rapid speciation events — challenging the gradualist picture of slow continuous change. What's the current view?
questions.answer: Punctuated equilibrium and gradualism are now generally seen as complementary patterns — both occurring at different scales and in different lineages, rather than as mutually exclusive alternatives in evolutionary biology
choices: Punctuated equilibrium and gradualism are now generally seen as complementary patterns — both occurring at different scales and in different lineages, rather than as mutually exclusive alternatives in evolutionary biology
Punctuated equilibrium has been formally refuted — by every paleontological study since the 1990s, and Gould himself retracted the position in his major 2002 book before his death in the same year

Punctuated equilibrium has replaced gradualism entirely — and is now the only accepted model of evolutionary change, with the gradualist framework taught only as historical context in introductory biology courses

Punctuated equilibrium and gradualism are identical — and the Eldredge-Gould paper turned out to be merely a restatement of standard Darwinian theory under different terminology than was previously employed
questions.context: Eldredge and Gould drew on the fossil record's tendency to show long species lifetimes (stasis) followed by relatively rapid replacement (punctuation). The pattern is real in many lineages. Gradualists like Richard Dawkins argued that 'rapid' on geological timescales can still be many generations of selection. The current synthesis treats the rate of evolution as varying across lineages, environments, and life-history characteristics. Both stasis and rapid change are real features of the fossil record.

questions.question: The bacterial flagellum is a rotary motor — a corkscrew tail driven by an actual molecular motor embedded in the cell wall. It's been used as an example by intelligent-design advocates of 'irreducible complexity.' What's the current evolutionary understanding?
questions.answer: Comparative genomic studies have identified plausible precursor structures — including the type III secretion system, which uses many of the same proteins for a simpler function, making stepwise evolution plausible though not fully reconstructed
choices: Comparative genomic studies have identified plausible precursor structures — including the type III secretion system, which uses many of the same proteins for a simpler function, making stepwise evolution plausible though not fully reconstructed

The bacterial flagellum has been shown to be impossible to evolve — by every formal study since the 1990s, and modern biology now accepts that natural selection alone cannot account for its development from earlier structures

The bacterial flagellum was assembled by direct intelligent design — and modern biology has formally accepted this conclusion, with all major textbooks now teaching it as the standard explanation for the structure

The bacterial flagellum is not actually a rotary motor — and the original claim was based on a mistaken interpretation of the electron microscope images that has since been retracted by the original observers
questions.context: The 'irreducible complexity' argument (Michael Behe, *Darwin's Black Box*, 1996) claimed that systems requiring many interacting parts could not have evolved gradually because removing any part disables the whole. The argument has been criticized on multiple grounds. The flagellum example specifically is now reasonably well-understood in evolutionary terms — though the full stepwise history is not pinned down. Honest summary: science doesn't pretend the full history is known, but the 'cannot evolve' claim has been answered.

questions.question: The Wright Brothers' first powered flight was at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903. The biology of flight had been studied for centuries by then — birds, bats, insects all fly. Yet ornithologists in the late 1800s widely believed powered human flight was impossible. What's the recognition skill?
questions.answer: Established biological knowledge does not automatically translate to engineering possibilities — a thing being unknown in nature does not make it impossible, a pattern that recurs throughout the history of applied science
choices: Established biological knowledge does not automatically translate to engineering possibilities — a thing being unknown in nature does not make it impossible, a pattern that recurs throughout the history of applied science

The Wright Brothers were not actually scientists — and their flight was a hoax until verified independently in the 1950s, with no formal recognition by aerospace scientists until after the Second World War

Bird flight and airplane flight use identical mechanisms — and the Wright Brothers' design copied bird wings exactly, with no engineering innovation required to enable powered heavier-than-air human flight

Powered flight was actually invented by Leonardo da Vinci — in the late 1400s, with the Wright Brothers' contribution being only a minor refinement of da Vinci's complete original design that had been forgotten
questions.context: Sir George Cayley laid the engineering principles for fixed-wing aircraft in 1799 — over a century before the Wrights. Otto Lilienthal flew gliders in the 1890s and was killed in one in 1896. Samuel Pierpont Langley, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, tried to build powered aircraft and failed. The Wrights' contribution was three-axis control. Biological flight uses flapping wings; aircraft use fixed wings with separate engines. The recognition skill: nature has not always shown us all the engineering options.

questions.question: Convergent evolution is the independent emergence of similar features in distantly related lineages — the camera eye of squids and vertebrates, echolocation in bats and dolphins, powered flight in insects, pterosaurs, birds, and bats. What does convergence tell us about biological design?
questions.answer: Some solutions are favored by physics and selection regardless of lineage — and convergent features tell us about what's possible and useful, even when evolution proceeded independently in different groups
choices: Some solutions are favored by physics and selection regardless of lineage — and convergent features tell us about what's possible and useful, even when evolution proceeded independently in different groups

Convergent evolution proves all species are genetically identical — and modern taxonomy is artificial, with no real differences between any of the species shown to have evolved similar features through convergence

Convergent evolution disproves natural selection — by showing random variation could not produce similar outcomes in multiple lineages, refuting Darwin's framework for biological diversity on convergence evidence

Convergent evolution is a mathematical certainty — and modern biology shows any trait must evolve in every possible lineage given enough time, regardless of selection pressures or genetic constraints whatsoever
questions.context: Eyes are an especially well-studied case. Camera eyes in vertebrates and cephalopods have similar structure but very different developmental origins — and the camera eye is just one of about a dozen independent eye-evolution events. The lens-based eye is convergent across many lineages. Echolocation in dolphins and bats shows convergence at the molecular level — the same gene (Prestin) has the same key mutations in both groups, an example of 'molecular convergence' that surprised researchers.

questions.question: Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, sent Charles Darwin a manuscript in 1858 that independently described natural selection. Darwin had been sitting on his own work for over two decades. How did they handle the priority dispute?
questions.answer: Darwin's friends arranged a joint presentation at the Linnean Society in July 1858 — with both men's contributions read aloud the same evening, and Darwin published *On the Origin of Species* the following year as the major statement
choices: Darwin's friends arranged a joint presentation at the Linnean Society in July 1858 — with both men's contributions read aloud the same evening, and Darwin published *On the Origin of Species* the following year as the major statement

Darwin claimed sole credit for the theory — and Wallace was ignored for the remainder of his life, with no recognition of his independent discovery until decades after his death from natural causes in 1913

Wallace claimed sole credit and published the first paper — with Darwin's work appearing only years later as a popularization of Wallace's earlier and more rigorous formulation of the theory of natural selection
The two men sued each other in British court — over the priority dispute, leading to a famous decade-long trial that established the modern legal framework for scientific priority disputes used today
questions.context: Wallace's 1858 letter, sent from the island of Ternate to Darwin in England, prompted the joint Linnean Society presentation. Wallace was never bitter about Darwin's greater fame; he wrote *Darwinism* (1889) acknowledging Darwin's deeper development of the theory. Both men published much else over their lifetimes; Wallace also developed early ideas in biogeography (the 'Wallace Line' separating Asian and Australian fauna). The case illustrates how scientific priority can be handled gracefully when the parties have collegial relationships.

questions.question: The 'Modern Synthesis' of the 1930s-1940s integrated Mendelian genetics with Darwinian natural selection. Since around 2010, some biologists have advocated an 'Extended Evolutionary Synthesis' (EES), arguing the original framework misses important factors. What do EES advocates propose adding?
questions.answer: Niche construction, developmental plasticity, epigenetic inheritance, and inclusive fitness — among other factors that influence how variation is generated and propagated beyond simple gene-frequency change in populations
choices: Niche construction, developmental plasticity, epigenetic inheritance, and inclusive fitness — among other factors that influence how variation is generated and propagated beyond simple gene-frequency change in populations

Direct divine intervention — and miraculous appearances of new species, which advocates argue must be included to explain features that natural selection cannot account for, regardless of any evidence to the contrary

The complete rejection of natural selection — and replacement with a different mechanism entirely, in a move that has been endorsed by every major evolutionary biology department since the year 2015 everywhere

Only one tiny correction to a single equation — that had no effect on biology in practice, with the Extended Evolutionary Synthesis being identical in every meaningful respect to the original Modern Synthesis
questions.context: The EES debate is real and is internal to evolutionary biology. Critics including Richard Dawkins, Jerry Coyne, and Douglas Futuyma have argued that the Modern Synthesis already accommodates most of what EES advocates name. EES proponents (Kevin Laland, Eva Jablonka, Marion Lamb, Denis Noble) argue the original framework systematically underweights certain factors. The debate is professional, not religious. The bank covers it honestly as an open question about emphasis rather than as 'evolution is wrong.'

questions.question: For decades, the majority of the human genome — the parts that don't code for proteins — was widely described as 'junk DNA.' In September 2012, the ENCODE Project Consortium published a series of papers in *Nature* and other journals making a much stronger claim. What did ENCODE say?
questions.answer: About 80% of the genome has 'biochemical function' — based on assays showing transcription, chromatin marks, or transcription factor binding, in a finding that sparked immediate methodological debate about what 'function' means
choices: About 80% of the genome has 'biochemical function' — based on assays showing transcription, chromatin marks, or transcription factor binding, in a finding that sparked immediate methodological debate about what 'function' means

About 99% of the genome is junk DNA — with no remaining doubt about the term, and the ENCODE Project itself concluded the 'junk DNA' label was correct after a decade of follow-up research and reanalysis

The human genome contains exactly 30,000 genes — a finding that has been refined precisely to four decimal places by ENCODE and is no longer the subject of any methodological dispute among working geneticists

All non-protein-coding DNA is identical — between humans and bananas, with no significant variation across species, in a result that has reshaped the entire field of comparative genomics for the modern era
questions.context: ENCODE's 80% claim was widely reported and criticized. Critics including Dan Graur argued ENCODE conflated 'biochemical activity' with 'biological function' — noisy transcription doesn't mean useful function. Estimates of truly functional non-coding DNA in humans range from about 8% to 25% depending on how 'function' is defined. The 'junk DNA' framework has been substantially revised: much non-coding DNA does have regulatory roles. But the strong 80% claim was overconfident.

questions.question: Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression that don't involve changes to the DNA sequence itself — DNA methylation, histone modification, non-coding RNA regulation. The field has grown enormously since around 2000. What's a recurring overstatement to watch for?
questions.answer: 'Lamarckian inheritance' — claims that environmental exposures of one generation can directly drive heritable epigenetic changes in the next, sometimes overstated, but real transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is documented in some specific systems
choices: 'Lamarckian inheritance' — claims that environmental exposures of one generation can directly drive heritable epigenetic changes in the next, sometimes overstated, but real transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is documented in some specific systems

'Epigenetics is identical to genetics' — and there's nothing new about it, in a position that has been endorsed by every major geneticist working in the field since around the year 2010 in any country

'Epigenetics doesn't exist at all' — and the entire field has been a hoax since its founding, with every published paper retracted and the term banned from textbooks across all major medical schools today

'Epigenetics fully replaces Darwinian inheritance' — and natural selection no longer applies, with all modern evolutionary biology built entirely on environmental rather than genetic mechanisms of change
questions.context: Some transgenerational epigenetic effects are real (Dutch Hunger Winter studies, agouti mouse coat-color experiments). But sweeping claims that 'epigenetics overturns Darwinism' or 'parents transmit their experiences to children' are exaggerated. The mechanism for stable multi-generation epigenetic transmission in mammals is limited; most epigenetic marks are erased and reset between generations. The recognition skill: distinguish 'real but limited' from 'paradigm-overturning' versions of the same claim.

questions.question: The Human Microbiome Project (NIH, 2007-2016) characterized the bacterial communities living in and on the human body. Bacteria outnumber human cells in our bodies by a ratio originally estimated at 10:1 — now refined to about 1.3:1. What's the recognition skill about how recent this is?
questions.answer: The field is younger than many doctors — and most clinical practice still doesn't account for microbiome effects on drug response, disease risk, or behavior, despite increasing evidence for real interactions across body systems
choices: The field is younger than many doctors — and most clinical practice still doesn't account for microbiome effects on drug response, disease risk, or behavior, despite increasing evidence for real interactions across body systems

The field has been mature for over a century — and microbiome effects are routinely integrated into all medical decisions, with every prescription written in the United States accounting for the patient's bacterial flora

The field was discontinued in 2018 — after no clinically useful findings emerged, and the Human Microbiome Project formally concluded that microbiome studies have no medical relevance whatsoever in any setting

The field has only existed since 2023 — and so few discoveries have been made that no recognition skill is yet possible in this area of modern biological research and biomedical investigation more broadly
questions.context: The microbiome field really did begin in earnest around 2007 — high-throughput DNA sequencing made it possible to identify the bacteria in samples without growing them. Strong evidence now links the gut microbiome to inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, mental health, immune development, drug metabolism, and antibiotic effects. But translation to clinical practice is slow. The 10:1 figure was an overestimate; the 1.3:1 figure (Sender, Fuchs, Milo 2016) is more accurate.

questions.question: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) — transferring fecal material from a healthy donor into a patient's gut — has become standard of care for recurrent *Clostridium difficile* infection. Cure rates often exceed 90% — far higher than any antibiotic. What's the recognition skill about FMT?
questions.answer: The treatment was practiced informally for years before formal acceptance — with strong evidence from small trials that mainstream medicine resisted, until the magnitude of benefit became too large to ignore
choices: The treatment was practiced informally for years before formal acceptance — with strong evidence from small trials that mainstream medicine resisted, until the magnitude of benefit became too large to ignore

The treatment was developed exclusively in pharmaceutical labs — using purified compounds derived from microbiome research that had been funded by major drug companies starting in the year 2010 at earliest

The treatment has been formally banned by the FDA — and is illegal in all 50 US states, regardless of patient preference or physician recommendation, with no exceptions allowed under any current applicable regulation

The treatment was invented from scratch in 2020 — with no prior history of any kind, and has only been used in clinical trials of fewer than 30 patients each since the original randomized study was published
questions.context: The first modern FMT report was Eiseman 1958. Australian gastroenterologist Thomas Borody has been a major modern proponent since the 1980s. The procedure was widely viewed with skepticism until randomized controlled trials in the 2010s (van Nood et al. 2013) showed cure rates over 90% for recurrent C. difficile. FMT is now considered standard of care for that indication. Other applications (IBD, obesity, autism) are still under investigation.

questions.question: The gut-brain axis — bidirectional communication between the gut microbiome and the central nervous system — has emerged as one of the most active areas of microbiome research. What's the current state of the science?
questions.answer: Real but provisional — strong evidence for some specific mechanisms (vagal nerve signaling, microbial metabolites, immune modulation) but much popular reporting overclaims definite causal effects from limited observational data
choices: Real but provisional — strong evidence for some specific mechanisms (vagal nerve signaling, microbial metabolites, immune modulation) but much popular reporting overclaims definite causal effects from limited observational data

Fully established with no remaining uncertainty — every aspect of mental health is now explained by gut microbiome composition, and probiotics are the standard treatment for all psychiatric conditions worldwide

Refuted as an experimental artifact — no real communication exists between the gut and the brain beyond ordinary nutrient absorption, and all claims to the contrary have been retracted by the field as of 2022

An entirely new scientific revolution — that has overturned all prior neuroscience, with the brain now widely recognized as merely a secondary organ controlled directly by gut bacteria in every healthy person
questions.context: The mechanisms behind gut-brain interaction are real and being characterized — short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, vagal-nerve signaling, immune-cell migration. But the leap from 'gut microbes affect mood in some animal models' to 'change your gut and cure your depression' is much bigger than the evidence supports for most conditions. Honest reporting separates mechanistic findings from clinical applications. The field is active but young.

questions.question: Francis Crick's 'central dogma of molecular biology,' articulated in 1958 and again in 1970, stated the direction of information flow in cells: DNA → RNA → protein. Crick was careful in 1970 to clarify what he meant by the rule. What's the precise content?
questions.answer: Information cannot flow from protein back to nucleic acid — DNA-to-RNA and RNA-to-protein are well-established, with reverse transcription (RNA-to-DNA) discovered in 1970 and integrated into the framework that same year
choices: Information cannot flow from protein back to nucleic acid — DNA-to-RNA and RNA-to-protein are well-established, with reverse transcription (RNA-to-DNA) discovered in 1970 and integrated into the framework that same year

Information flows only in one direction at all times — and reverse transcription is a fabrication that has been refuted by every laboratory study attempted since the original announcement in 1970 anywhere

Information flows in every direction equally — including from protein back to DNA, with the central dogma being a misleading historical artifact that no modern molecular biologist actually accepts as valid today

Information cannot flow between cells at all — but transfers freely within a single cell, in a framework that explains the origin of multicellular life and the development of the immune system in vertebrate species
questions.context: Crick's actual 1970 *Nature* paper carefully distinguishes 'general transfers' (DNA-to-DNA replication, DNA-to-RNA transcription, RNA-to-protein translation, all known and accepted), 'special transfers' (reverse transcription, RNA replication, both real but limited), and 'unknown transfers' (protein-to-RNA, protein-to-DNA, protein-to-protein information transfer — not known to occur). The dogma is often misstated as 'DNA-only one-way' — Crick's actual statement was more careful and remains valid in its precise form.

questions.question: Watson, Crick, and Wilkins won the 1962 Nobel Prize for the DNA double helix. Rosalind Franklin had taken Photo 51 — the X-ray diffraction image that revealed the helix structure — but she died of ovarian cancer in 1958. Why did she not share the Nobel?
questions.answer: The Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously — and Franklin had died four years before the prize, though her contribution to identifying the structure is now widely acknowledged as central to the discovery
choices: The Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously — and Franklin had died four years before the prize, though her contribution to identifying the structure is now widely acknowledged as central to the discovery

The Nobel Committee determined her contribution was insufficient — and would not have awarded her the prize even had she been alive in 1962, regardless of her contribution to the X-ray analysis itself

Franklin refused to accept the Nobel Prize — on principle, given the conduct of Watson and Wilkins in publishing her data without permission, and her family carried out her stated refusal posthumously in 1962
Franklin was awarded the Nobel Prize separately — in chemistry rather than medicine, in a ceremony held in 1958 just before her death from the ovarian cancer that had ended her career a year earlier
questions.context: Photo 51 was taken by Franklin's PhD student Raymond Gosling in May 1952 at King's College London. Maurice Wilkins showed the photograph to Watson without Franklin's knowledge in 1953. The Cambridge group rapidly built the helix model on the structural information visible in Photo 51. Watson's later book *The Double Helix* (1968) presented Franklin unflatteringly; Anne Sayre's 1975 biography and modern reconsiderations have substantially restored her reputation.

questions.question: In November 2018, Chinese biophysicist He Jiankui announced he had used CRISPR-Cas9 to edit the embryos of twin girls, producing the first known live human births with deliberate germline gene edits. The international scientific community was overwhelmingly critical. What was the consensus reaction?
questions.answer: His work was widely condemned — for proceeding without proper informed consent, adequate safety review, or transparent peer evaluation, and he was sentenced to three years in prison by Chinese authorities in 2019
choices: His work was widely condemned — for proceeding without proper informed consent, adequate safety review, or transparent peer evaluation, and he was sentenced to three years in prison by Chinese authorities in 2019

His work was celebrated as a breakthrough — and he was awarded honorary professorships at several leading universities, with the scientific community lining up to endorse his approach to embryo editing

His work was widely accepted as routine — and gene-editing of embryos became standard medical practice within a year, with no major regulatory pushback in any country following his original announcement

His work was a hoax that never actually happened — and the announcement was retracted within weeks by relevant Chinese institutions, with no embryo editing having taken place at any time according to subsequent investigation
questions.context: He Jiankui claimed to have disabled the CCR5 gene in twin girls, aiming for resistance to HIV. The targeted edits did not work as planned — at least one twin appears to have CCR5 active. The international scientific community condemned the work as premature and unethical. He was sentenced to three years in prison. The episode prompted serious international discussions about germline editing governance — though no enforceable global regime has yet emerged.

questions.question: In December 2023, the FDA approved Casgevy — the first CRISPR-based therapy approved for clinical use. Developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals and CRISPR Therapeutics, it treats sickle-cell disease. What's the basic approach?
questions.answer: Patients' own bone-marrow stem cells are edited outside the body — to reactivate fetal hemoglobin production, then transplanted back, providing a one-time treatment for the genetic disorder rather than chronic management
choices: Patients' own bone-marrow stem cells are edited outside the body — to reactivate fetal hemoglobin production, then transplanted back, providing a one-time treatment for the genetic disorder rather than chronic management

Patients' embryos are edited before implantation — preventing the disease in future generations, with germline modifications routinely used in the United States since the Casgevy approval in late 2023 as standard care

Patients receive lifelong oral CRISPR doses — taken daily as a maintenance medication, with no surgical or cell-extraction component to the treatment regimen as approved by the FDA in late 2023 for clinical use

Patients receive a vaccine containing the CRISPR system — that finds and corrects the relevant genetic defect through their bloodstream, in a single injection that has replaced all prior sickle-cell disease treatments
questions.context: Casgevy uses ex vivo (outside the body) editing of the patient's own stem cells, then reinfuses them. The edit reactivates fetal hemoglobin production by disrupting BCL11A, a repressor of the fetal hemoglobin gene. Trials showed dramatic reduction in pain crises. The approach is somatic (only the patient's cells), not germline (no inherited changes). Casgevy is therapeutic gene editing — celebrated by the field as the promise CRISPR finally delivering on. The contested case is germline editing, as in He Jiankui.

questions.question: DeepMind's AlphaFold-2, released in 2021, made a major advance on the long-standing 'protein folding problem' — predicting how a sequence of amino acids folds into a three-dimensional structure. What had been the state of the field before AlphaFold-2?
questions.answer: Protein folding was a 50-year unsolved problem — with X-ray crystallography and NMR as the only reliable structural methods, and computational prediction from sequence had been an aspiration that had defeated multiple generations of researchers
choices: Protein folding was a 50-year unsolved problem — with X-ray crystallography and NMR as the only reliable structural methods, and computational prediction from sequence had been an aspiration that had defeated multiple generations of researchers

Protein folding was a fully solved problem since 1990 — and AlphaFold added nothing important to the field, with all major folds already predictable from sequence using methods developed in the early molecular biology era

Protein folding had never been studied seriously — until DeepMind started the AlphaFold project in 2018, with no prior tradition of any kind in the protein-structure-prediction area of computational biology

Protein folding has been declared impossible to predict — by every major biology textbook published since the year 1985, and AlphaFold's results have been formally retracted by the journal that published them
questions.context: AlphaFold-2 outperformed competing methods at the 2020 CASP14 protein-structure-prediction competition by a large margin. Predictions for many proteins were accurate enough to be useful for biological inference, sometimes rivaling experimental structures. The 2021 release of predictions for nearly every human protein and many others has been one of biology's most useful single resources of the 2020s. AlphaFold doesn't solve the protein-folding problem in physical detail — it learns from known structures — but it makes the field's central tool widely available.

questions.question: Proteomics — the systematic study of all proteins in a cell, tissue, or organism — emerged as a major field in the early 2000s, alongside genomics. Proteomes are far more variable than genomes. Why?
questions.answer: One gene can produce many protein variants through alternative splicing — post-translational modification, and degradation differences, so the proteome is much larger and more dynamic than the underlying genome
choices: One gene can produce many protein variants through alternative splicing — post-translational modification, and degradation differences, so the proteome is much larger and more dynamic than the underlying genome

Proteins are made directly from RNA without any genes involved — and so the proteome has no relationship to the genome, with the two being entirely independent regulatory systems in modern molecular biology

Proteomes are smaller than genomes by a factor of ten — and so they contain less information, with the typical human cell containing only a few thousand proteins despite the much larger gene count present
Proteomes are entirely identical to genomes — and the term 'proteome' is just an alternative name for the genome, used by researchers in countries that do not have a national protein research program
questions.context: The human genome contains about 20,000 protein-coding genes; estimated counts of distinct human protein species range from 100,000 to over a million depending on how variants are counted. Alternative splicing alone produces many protein variants per gene. Phosphorylation, glycosylation, and other modifications add further complexity. Mass spectrometry made proteome-scale analysis feasible. The field is now central to drug discovery, biomarker development, and clinical diagnostics.

questions.question: Telomeres are the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes — repetitive DNA sequences (TTAGGG repeats in humans) that shorten slightly with each cell division. Blackburn, Greider, and Szostak won the 2009 Nobel Prize for telomere research. What's a recurring overstatement in popular reporting?
questions.answer: 'Shorter telomeres cause aging' — telomere length correlates with cell aging and disease risk, but a stronger causal story is hard to pin down, and 'telomere extender' products marketed to consumers oversell the science
choices: 'Shorter telomeres cause aging' — telomere length correlates with cell aging and disease risk, but a stronger causal story is hard to pin down, and 'telomere extender' products marketed to consumers oversell the science
'Telomeres do not exist' — and the entire field has been a fabrication since the 2009 Nobel Prize, with no real biological basis for any claim published in the field of cellular biology around aging

'All cells have identical telomeres' — so the variation reported in the literature must be measurement error, with the telomere field having been formally retracted by the major journals since around 2018

'Telomere length is fixed at birth' — and never changes, with all the variation reported in adults being a fabrication created by laboratories competing for funding rather than a real biological observation
questions.context: Telomere biology is real and important — telomeres protect chromosome ends, telomerase extends them in germ cells and stem cells, cancer cells often reactivate telomerase. The connection to organismal aging is more complex than 'short telomeres = aging.' Consumer products claiming to 'restore telomere length' or measure 'biological age' from telomere length oversell the science. Working biologists treat telomere length as one of many biomarkers, not as the master clock of aging.

questions.question: In 2006 Japanese scientist Shinya Yamanaka discovered that four specific transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) could reprogram adult skin cells into pluripotent stem cells — cells capable of becoming any cell type. He shared the 2012 Nobel Prize with John Gurdon. Why was this discovery so important?
questions.answer: It eliminated the need for embryonic stem cells in many applications — sidestepping the major ethical controversy while opening new clinical possibilities for personalized regenerative medicine from each patient's own cells
choices: It eliminated the need for embryonic stem cells in many applications — sidestepping the major ethical controversy while opening new clinical possibilities for personalized regenerative medicine from each patient's own cells

It proved all cells are identical — and so any cell can be used in place of any other for medical purposes, in a finding that has eliminated the need for matching donors in transplantation medicine worldwide

It proved stem cells do not exist — and so all prior research in the field was fraudulent, with the Yamanaka Nobel awarded as a public-relations gesture rather than for any actual contribution to biology
It proved embryos are not needed for human reproduction — and so all reproduction can be carried out from adult skin samples, eliminating the need for both eggs and sperm in any context anywhere
questions.context: Yamanaka's iPSC method made it possible to derive pluripotent stem cells from any patient's own skin or blood, avoiding both the ethical controversy around embryonic stem cells and the immune-rejection issues of donor-derived cells. iPSC-derived therapies are now being developed for macular degeneration, Parkinson's disease, spinal-cord injury, and other conditions. The first clinical use of iPSC-derived cells in Japan (Mandai 2014, macular degeneration) marked the transition to clinical practice.

questions.question: The amyloid hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease — that beta-amyloid plaques cause the cognitive decline — has dominated the field since the late 1980s. Over $1 billion has been spent on amyloid-clearing drugs. The clinical results have been disappointing. What's the recognition skill?
questions.answer: Major drug-development efforts can rest on a hypothesis only partly correct — the field has been slow to take alternative hypotheses (vascular, infectious, mitochondrial) seriously, despite decades of disappointing trial results
choices: Major drug-development efforts can rest on a hypothesis only partly correct — the field has been slow to take alternative hypotheses (vascular, infectious, mitochondrial) seriously, despite decades of disappointing trial results

The amyloid hypothesis was confirmed in 2024 — and all alternatives have been ruled out by the latest clinical trials, with Aducanumab and Lecanemab providing definitive cures for early-stage Alzheimer's disease

Alzheimer's disease has been entirely cured since 2020 — and no further research is needed, with major pharmaceutical companies having moved on to other neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's and Huntington's
